speechtext:
The objectives of this bill are spelled out in considerable detail in the explanatory note, so in the interests of brevity and with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote from the first paragraph:
This bill provides for a United Nations cooperative credit union whereby more than 100 nations may buy the food and agricultural products of Canada on term credit: and by so distributing these products, actively contribute toward an expanding world economy, vitally strengthen Canada's position in the food market of the world, and assure a rising standard of living for Canada's farmers, fishermen and forest workers; and, in so far as revolution marches on an empty stomach, contribute to world peace.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, November 16, consideration of the motion of Miss LaMarsh for the second reading of Bill No. C-136, to establish a comprehensive program of old age pensions and supplementary benefits in Canada payable to and in respect of contributors.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
There are many matters which could be discussed on the second reading of this bill, but what we are really deciding now on second reading are not questions of detail. In normal circumstances we would be deciding whether or not to accept the principle or principles of the bill.
In this particular case we are presented with an unusual situation. After second reading the measure before us is to be referred to a special committee of this house and of the Senate where the whole subject of the pension plan is to be considered not only in detail but in principle. This committee, when

Canada Pension Plan
it starts its work, will have unusually broad powers if we accept the statements of the Prime Minister in this regard, and the indications given in the correspondence which has been filed.
Earlier this year I requested certain information in motion No. 101, and this information was filed in sessional paper No. 202G of May 8, 1964. It consisted of letters and telegrams sent by the Prime Minister, as well as statements made by him, outlining the duties of the committee it was intended to set up. I should like to mention two of these documents in particular because they give a clear indication of the government's intentions with regard to the work of the committee. The first is a letter sent from Ottawa and dated March 4, 1964. It is addressed to a Mr. Higgins whose address is given. In the course of this letter the Prime Minister makes the following statement:
The committee will have full power to hear the advice of interested organizations and to make any recommendations, of principle as well as of detail, concerning a pension plan-including, indeed, the recommendation if it so wishes that the plan as proposed should be fundamentally revised.
There was a second letter, also from Ottawa, dated February 22, 1964 and sent to a Mr. Mitchell, and I should like to quote from this as well. Incidentally, both these letters are signed by the Prime Minister. It says:
The committee will have full power to hear the advice of interested organizations and to make any recommendations, of principle as well as of detail, concerning a pension plan-including, indeed, the recommendation if it so wished that the plan as proposed should be fundamentally revised.
There are a number of other letters to the same effect, but I think the idea is clearly expressed in those two quotations; that this bill, when it goes to the committee, will be examined not only in detail but fundamentally. It seems to me therefore that all we have to decide in this house at the present time is whether or not a pension plan is desirable. While we may discuss many other things on second reading, the extremely broad powers given to the committee leave us with this single question to be decided. The effective date, the amount of contributions and payments, whether this is to be a pay as you go or a funded plan, the question of who would be included or excluded, are all, I believe, still subject to revision at the hands of the special committee.
With this in mind I should like to proceed to deal with another topic, one which concerns the time element the committee will

have to face. We now have before us a bill of 125 clauses as compared to the 88 clauses of the previous bill. It is admittedly a complex measure whose effects will reach far into the future. The bill itself was only made public in its revised form a very few days ago. There are many organizations, both public and private, which wish to study the legislation in its new form and appear before the committee for the purpose of making recommendations.
I can hardly believe that the committee will be able to complete its hearings by the end of the present session or in the four or five weeks which are left ahead of us. If it tries to do so it will be doing an inefficient and incomplete job. I believe many of the organizations to which I have referred would require many weeks to examine the bill, discuss its implications and prepare briefs for presentation to the committee. It seems to me that the government has allowed itself to get into a time problem, but this should not be permitted to derogate from the importance of the bill itself. I hope, therefore, that the government does not expect the committee to rush the bill through in the course of the current session.
Arrangements will have to be made, I think, in one of two ways. Either there should be provision for the committee to carry on its work during the next session or, alternatively, the government should arrange for the bill to be renewed at the beginning of the next session. Members of the committee could proceed now to hold preliminary discussions and hear explanations by departmental officials until the end of the current session. Then by agreement the bill could be renewed at the beginning of next session when the same committee could be set up to carry on the work which had been interrupted. I do not think we should ask or expect the special committee to finish its work during the present session.
I should like now to discuss a technical problem in connection with the special committee. We have set up a joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons, and I think there will be no great difficulty with respect to the members of this house who have been chosen. The bill will have had its second reading in this house and will have been referred to the committee.
But I should like to ask this question. What is the position of the members of that committee who come from the Senate? They will be considering a bill which will not even have been introduced into the other place, let

alone given approval in principle. The procedure now being followed assumes that the Senate will give second reading to the bill, and I think that is assuming a great deal. What will be the position of a senator who sits on this committee and takes part in a complete revision and overhaul of the bill before us as a result of which a report is made to the House of Commons? Where will he stand when the bill comes up in the Senate? Where will the Senate itself stand if a majority of its members does not agree with the work done by the committee of which representatives from the other place formed a part? They will have considered the form, the effect and the detail of the bill before ever having discussed or passed upon the principle.
There is a more practical aspect involved. To whom will the joint committee report? I assume it will report to the House of Commons, after which I suppose the measure will be considered in committee by the whole house and read the third time. But the committee could not send its first report to the other place because, first of all, the senators do not have the bill before them and in the second place they will not be set up for the purpose of reporting. I ask, if questions are raised in the other place on second reading, does the bill go back to the joint committee again?
These are not just rhetorical questions, Mr. Speaker, or raising difficulties; I see this as a real difficulty with regard to the procedure that has been adopted. No matter how you go about it there is this assumption that the other place is going to go along with whatever the House of Commons does and whatever its committee recommends. I assume that the gentlemen in the other place will have something to say about this, but I believe it should be said here also; because there is a serious problem involved in the assumption that the Senate will be automatic in their concurrence in the principle of this bill. We certainly know there are gentlemen in the other place who have very serious doubts about the whole question of priorities, as have some hon. members in this house, and we will not have had the opportunity of testing that opinion in the other place before we go into the special committee.
There is another matter, Mr. Speaker, that has already been raised briefly. It is also a technical problem and relates to the provisions for amendment of the act. I refer to the provision that requires two thirds of the provinces having two thirds of the population
Canada Pension Plan
to be consulted and approve of any change in the bill. This bill is a simple enactment of the parliament of Canada. It requires no approval by any of the provinces because by an amendment to the British North America Act they have given this parliament power to legislate on questions of pensions, survivor benefits and disability allowances. Therefore it requires no consent for its passage; it requires no consent for its repeal.
I think it is a well understood principle that no parliament can bind a future parliament in this way. I suggest that if the government wants to make it binding on future parliaments that the provinces must be consulted and must agree to amendments to this bill, that would have to be done by way of approval of an agreement between the federal government and the provincial governments. By this means an agreement would be ratified which would become binding on future parliaments and would be effective in the event that this is a desirable provision. But as it now stands I think the inclusion of this particular provision is worthless and empty, because I see no reason why next year or in any future session of parliament this particular section of the bill could not be repealed and there would be no need to consult any of the provinces to so repeal it. I believe it is merely a unilateral declaration of intention and nothing else.
But, Mr. Speaker, going beyond the mere form of the amending principle, we have to ask whether such a restriction is desirable; that is, that the parliament of Canada would be unable, if it so desired, to amend an act of parliament which had not had the approval of another legislative body. I presume that the objective is portability; that this is written into the bill in order that there may be some evenness in pension legislation across the country so that before the federal parliament makes amending provisions the provinces shall have been consulted and shall have agreed. If that is the intention I do not believe that result is achieved, because the section only affects those provinces which will be in the plan and specifically, as I understand it now in any case, it will not include the province of Quebec. So if the desire is to deal with the question of portability, surely we cannot accomplish it by merely requiring the consent of two thirds of the provinces having two thirds of the population. Since Quebec is not in the plan it would not have to be consulted, and the whole question of portability across the country would be thrown out of gear very simply.

Canada Pension Plan
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, if it is portability that is desired by this clause, it cannot be achieved in this manner. If it is a case of the contributions being agreed to by the provinces, I cannot see that having the agreement of two thirds of the provinces with two thirds of the population will achieve this result either; you are still going to have a number of the provinces which presumably do not agree but are going to be forced into this position. Therefore it is not going to be a general agreement across the country at all; it is merely going to be a majority decision. For this reason I cannot, personally, see that the effect has been legally achieved in the bill that we have before us; and second, even if it could be, I doubt whether it is a desirable provision and whether it will achieve the result that the draftsmen of the bill have suggested. I think it fails on all these grounds. While that is not a good reason for rejecting the bill, I think it is a question which deserves very serious consideration in the committee.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, there are many questions which have to be asked about the effect and detail of this bill. We do not have, for example, the economic report which has been requested concerning the effect of the bill. The fact that the minister is keeping this report for the committee strengthens my belief and contention that the committee has basic powers of amendment or rejection in principle; because if the committee is to consider the economic effect of this pension plan on the country as a whole, surely the committee is considering the principle of the bill and the question of whether a pension plan of the magnitude that is now proposed is really desirable.
I think a large number of things have been done backwards in this bill. I think the committee will have trouble with it, and that there will be technical difficulties as between the Senate and House of Commons members of the committee. I think it is not in accordance with the basic fundamentals of the scheme that the economic effect of the pension plan should be studied by the committee. Surely this should normally be done on second reading, when we are discussing the principle of the bill.
Therefore I take the view, as do I think all my colleagues, that on second reading we are falling short of what should be decided in consideration of a public bill. Rather we are deciding, as in the case of private bills which come before the house, the mere question whether or not this is a bill which ought
(Mr. Aiken.]
to be given consideration. On that ground alone there could be no objection to this course. If any limitations were imposed on the committee I think we would have the right to insist on more complete discussion on second reading; but with the complete freedom of the committee to consider the whole problem, including the economic effects of the bill, I believe that most of these questions can be left until the bill has gone to the committee.

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us one of the major pieces of social legislation in Canada's history. It is a pleasure and a privilege for me, as I am sure it is for other hon. members, to be in a position to support it wholeheartedly.
The objective of the Canada pension plan can be stated quite simply. It will provide the community with a means by which the people who are working can assist, or support, those who are no longer able to do so. The Canada pension plan will assure those who are unable to work, the aged and the disabled, that they can live in decency and dignity.
A secondary result of the Canada pension plan will be the accumulation of funds for many years at least, which will be available for pressing social capital needs. Everyone recognizes the urgency of making available more technical and vocational schools, more hospitals, greater urban redevelopment schemes, expanded street and highway systems, and more university buildings. All these are the responsibility of provincial and municipal governments, and these governments will be greatly assisted by the accumulation of capital which will become available as a by-product of this social security scheme.
The Canada pension plan is a logical culmination of one of the major social trends evident in any industrialized society. This is the trend toward the maintenance of separate family units for each generation in the family. In rural societies, in more traditional societies, older people or those who for some reason or other are unable to work are cared for by the immediate family, usually in the home of that family. But as the community becomes more industrialized and the family becomes less of an economic unit, we have seen a trend away from this kind of social organization. It is true that many older people remain with their families or are assisted by them; but I think it is fair to say that most older people now come to be supported by other means. One of these is charity; another

takes the form of social aid provided by the state, including, in Canada, the old age security scheme; and still another is the provision of retirement benefits by pension or annuity plans.
But this mixed approach has not been adequate; indeed it has become increasingly unacceptable to the Canadian community. Even now only about 30 per cent of the labour force is covered by private pension plans, and some of these plans provide very small pensions indeed. Social aid is an important adjunct of these plans but the community has never really been satisfied that this is the appropriate form of assistance for people who are no longer able to work. The same is true of charitable support.
Consequently there has developed over the years a growing insistence that a comprehensive public pension plan be developed to meet the basic retirement needs of all Canadians. In 1927 the Canadian government began paying old age pensions on the basis of need, and in 1952 it established the old age security scheme for all people over 70 and began to contribute toward the support of people between the ages of 65 and 70 who were in need.
The Canada pension plan is the logical next step in the provision of a national pension plan. It will provide Canadians with an adequate retirement pension, not one which will finance a high standard of living but a reasonably adequate one. It will remain for the private pension plans to supplement the basic pensions paid through the Canada pension plan; their contribution will be to bring the standard of living of retired people up to the level they want, or have been able to provide through their other savings.
Now I shall say only a brief word about the secondary result which the Canada pension plan will achieve. Everyone recognizes the urgency of Canada's social capital needs, and I think there is a general consensus-I hope there is-that there should be a greater flow of capital in the direction of education, transportation, health and urban development. There is no suggestion that the plan should be fully funded, but in a pension plan which has reasonable contribution rates and which has a transitional period during which pension benefits are built up to their ultimate level there will be some accumulation of capital funds. These funds will be made available to the governments which are responsible for financing the various pressing social capital needs to which I have referred.
Canada Pension Plan
Hon. members on both sides of the house look forward, I am sure, to the introduction of this truly national pension plan. It will be a tribute to federal-provincial co-operation and a manifestation of national unity. In fact the plan in its present form was agreed to with the interests of national unity uppermost in mind. Canadians or their survivors in all provinces will receive exactly the same benefits on retirement or disability. They will be able to move from one province to another with complete freedom; in other words, there will be the kind of portability that my hon. friend was questioning just a few minutes ago. This in itself is an important and necessary factor in the preservation of our national unity.
There are, of course, opponents of the Canada pension plan. They have attacked it on a number of grounds. One of these is that it will discourage thrift, that everyone should provide their own pensions through their own savings. The point which these opponents miss, it seems to me, is that everyone will be doing this under the Canada pension plan in considerable measure, only they will not be doing it through private channels. Each generation while working will be contributing to the pensions of retired people, and in return the next generation will contribute to their pensions when they retire. This is simply a different method, and it seems to me a very sensible one, for an individual to provide for his retirement.
What these opponents of this plan really mean, I think, is that they would like to see these pensions provided not by governments but through privately controlled financial institutions. The truth is, however, that private pension plans cannot do what public plans can do, provide for the kind of intergeneration transfers which I have mentioned. Moreover, a large percentage of Canadians have been unable or have felt unable to provide adequately for their retirement through private plans.
But the main criticism advanced against the Canada pension plan, and the one I should like to discuss for a few minutes, is that Canada cannot afford it. I have often wondered what these critics mean when they say we cannot afford this plan. I am sure they cannot be suggesting that the younger generation should not be asked to contribute toward the retirement of older people, that the younger people cannot afford to do this, on the understanding, of course, that succeeding generations will contribute to their retirement. For it is surely possible, given the

Canada Pension Plan
standard of living that most working Canadians enjoy, for a working man to contribute for this purpose $1.80 a month for each $100 he earns over the basic $50 exemption, subject of course to the built-in maximum.
I suggest it is rather more likely that the critics do not really mean that we cannot afford the plan; rather they are predicting that its consequences would be to weaken the economy and to make all Canadians poorer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Is there a difference?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will wait a moment I will carry on and perhaps I will convince him, but I know his point of view and I am not so sure of that. For our part, we believe that Canadians can afford the plan if they want to, and we believe that the great majority of Canadians do want to. It is of course a question of personal priorities. In the opinion of members on this side of the house provision for our older generation is entitled to a high priority.
Let me describe the essence of the plan in economic terms. I think this can best be done by speaking of it as it will be when the benefits come to equal the contributions. This is the position we likely will be in some 20 years from now. The figures I will be using will refer to the estimated aggregate effect of the Canada pension plan as it would operate in nine provinces, plus the Quebec plan which will be virtually identical to the Canada plan.
When benefits come to equal contributions, income will simply be transferred from the active members of the labour force to those who are retired, as far as employee contributions are concerned. This transfer should lead to an increase in consumer demand since retired people need to spend and do spend an even larger proportion of their pensions than working people do of their wages. To the extent that this happens we will have provided the kind of floor to consumer expenditures which is desirable in a growing economy.
The consequence of higher levels of consumer expenditures is, of course, a relative reduction in personal savings. This is true to the extent that the active working people reduce their savings as a result of having made pension plan contributions. The effect of this must not be exaggerated, however. Total individual contributions in 1966 will be about one eighth of personal savings, that is, about 12J per cent. It would be surprising indeed if personal savings were to be reduced by as much as 5 per cent of what they would

have been were the Canada pension plan not in effect.
In the long run, that is, after the initial adjustments, it is highly unlikely that the rate of personal saving will be reduced at all. Certainly this has not been the case in other countries which have introduced social security schemes. In Canada the rate of personal saving has remained roughly unchanged despite the introduction of old age pensions, family allowances and other social security measures.
As for the consequences of the employer contributions, the adjustments required of the business community are not as great as some people have suggested. Business costs will, of course, increase. But the increase will not be substantial. Indeed I would guess that it will not amount to more than 1 per cent of payrolls. I point out that the contribution rate of 1.8 per cent does not apply to incomes below $600 or to those above $5,000. The effective average rate will be about 1 per cent. When you compare this one time 1 per cent increase in business payrolls-I repeat this is only a one time 1 per cent increase- with the repeated average annual increases in wages amounting to 3 or 4 per cent of payroll, which we have seen in recent years, you can only conclude that this will be a relatively minor adjustment. Moreover, increases in productivity normally enable business to absorb the higher costs without raising prices.
I freely acknowledge, however, that the pension plan contributions must in the short run be absorbed either by a reduction in profits or by price increases or by the negotiation of smaller wage increases than would otherwise have been granted. But again I must emphasize the magnitudes involved. The whole of the employers' contributions will not exceed 4 per cent of estimated profits after taxes and I simply do not believe that all of these contributions will be absorbed through reductions in profits.
Some businesses will pass on this cost. Where they did so through higher prices, total real consumption would rise at a slower rate, thus offsetting in part the increase in consumer demand brought about by higher pensions. The same effect would be felt if, instead of price increases, wage increases were restrained. But let me remind hon. members again of the magnitudes involved. The whole of employer contributions to the Canada pension plan, including the Quebec plan, will likely be only about one half of 1 per cent of the gross national product in 1966.

This leads me to say a word about our international competitive position. The government is very much aware of the role that the improvement in our international position has played in our present expansion. We have done this in part through maintaining relative price and cost stability while the price levels of our overseas competitors have been rising. In these circumstances our export and import competing industries will surely be in a position to absorb the minor increases in costs which I have just outlined.
So far I have been talking largely about the economic effects of the Canada pension plan when the benefits come to equal contributions, that is to say, the long term effect. The difference between this and the short run can be simply stated. Instead of the whole of the contributions being transferred to retired people, part of them will remain in the Canada pension fund, a large part in the early years of the plan. The economic question here is what happens to these funds.
The transfer in 1966 of some $550 million to $600 million, including Quebec, from individuals and businesses to public pension funds would, on the face of it, seem to have deflationary consequences. However, one must trace through all of the economic results in order to perceive the true effect of the transfer. For the apparent deflationary consequences will be offset by three factors: the reduction in government revenues that flows from deducting pension contributions from taxable income, the extent to which private savings have simply been transferred into public hands, and the effect that increased availability of loan capital may have on provincial and municipal capital spending. I should like to elaborate on each of these factors.
First, it must be recognized that the $550 million to $600 million that will be paid into public pension funds in 1966 is not the true measure of the extent to which private purchasing power will have been reduced. One must deduct from this figure the reduction in taxes that would otherwise have been payable by the individuals and businesses concerned. It is estimated that in 1966 individuals and businesses will reduce their tax payments to the federal and provincial governments by approximately $100 million as a result of charging their pension contributions against their taxable income.
Second, it must be recognized that a part of the public pension funds will represent simply a transfer of private savings to public savings. Put another way, we can expect that
20220-643J
Canada Pension Plan
in the short run there will be a slight reduction in the private savings in favour of the savings which will flow into public pension funds.
It is clearly impossible, as I said earlier, to estimate the magnitude of this effect on private savings, but to the extent that private savings are replaced by public savings the deflationary effect of the introduction of the public pension plans will be reduced.
The third factor to which I earlier referred is the possibility, perhaps I should say the probability, that provincial and municipal governments would increase capital spending as a result of the availability of more loan capital. The need for schools, urban development and redevelopment, highways and streets and other important categories of expenditure, is so great that this result is entirely possible. Indeed it has been represented to us, and to previous governments, that provinces and municipalities have been hampered in undertaking social capital projects by a shortage of loan capital. If in fact these governments do respond to the availability of capital in the pension funds by increasing their capital expenditures, then there will be a smaller adjustment for the economy to make than would otherwise have been anticipated.
There is another point that should be mentioned, and that is the effect the plan may have on the level of interest rates. To the extent that private savings are not reduced by the full extent of the new public savings, or to put this another way, to the extent that aggregate savings increase, one would reasonably anticipate a reduction in interest rates. This would tend to result in higher public and private investment, the magnitude of which is impossible to predict. This would be a further offset to the deflationary effect of the accumulation of the funds.
It will be apparent to hon. members from this analysis that any deflationary effect of the Canada pension plan in its present form will be far less than might appear at first glance. In contrast, the deflationary effects of a fully funded plan, as originally advocated by some people, would have been very serious indeed. If I have the time, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a further word at the conclusion of these remarks about the kind of results that might have flowed from this fully funded plan.
Inevitably there will be social and economic changes resulting from the introduction of the Canada pension plan. But these must be considered in the perspective of a rapidly expanding economy. It will be the respon-

Canada Pension Plan
sibility of government to ensure that the rate of growth of the Canadian economy is not interrupted.
I should like to conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying that our thinking has been based on two major premises. The first is that concern for older people is a valid and a high priority. The second is that an economy which is growing rapidly, as ours is and has the capacity to do, can easily make the adjustments that are required in order to give effect to this concern. The evidence supports this view. It cannot be said that the Canada pension plan will seriously impair the capability of businesses to generate new funds for expansion, or distort the structure of costs and prices, or impair the country's international competitive standing. Nor is there any evidence that social insurance programs of this nature inevitably cause a slowdown in economic growth. We are fortunate that the Canadian economy, and the Canadian people are capable of paying adequate pensions to older people. This is a noble endeavour in which all of us should be pleased to participate.
If I have a moment or two longer, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a further word about the original proposal of a fully funded plan. A fully funded plan would, of course, be one in which the initial contribution rate would be good for all time. I have indicated why such complete funding would not be good economics in a nation-wide plan. The partially funded plan that is proposed is, I believe, quite reasonable. It has, of course, the implications which the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) pointed out yesterday. Since we do not have complete funding, the time will come when the contribution rate may have to be raised. When that time will be, no one who understands the uncertainties of these matters will claim to be able to predict exactly. What we can say is that, at the contribution rate proposed, this plan will continue to generate funds-the income from contributions and interest on investments will exceed the outgo in contributions-for at least 20 years. That is true on even the most conservative of the chief actuary's estimates. All of those estimates are designed to avoid the danger of underestimating the cost of the plan. It is quite possible, even within the fairly conservative range of estimates, that the fund will go on growing into the 1990's. In other words, it will be fully a generation hence, perhaps more than that, before our successors have to decide to what extent they want to

continue partial funding of the plan. Obviously they will make that decision according to economic circumstances which none of us can now claim to predict. The one thing we can say is that, even at that point, the change in contribution rate that may be made 20, 25 or 30 years from now is not likely to be a big increase. That, again, is true even on the conservative projections of the cost. If those projections should turn out to be right, the rate might go up by a quarter or a third. That is to say, it would still be under 2\ per cent each for the employee and the employer. That would remain a modest price to pay for the benefits in security and social insurance which this plan provides.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am always interested in the statements and observations of my friend, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon). I always find myself in hearty agreement with all his objectives, but am always saddened by the fact that when the issue is joined the minister has an attack of caution and moves back and largely counteracts the benefits he has been foreseeing.
I felt that very much in his presentation this afternoon. He appeared to be spending a great deal of time reassuring the house that this pension plan is not going to have very much effect, is not going to disturb the economy in any way, is not going to move society in any particular earth-shaking manner, and that it will provide-I do not think even he was prepared to say comfortable pensions for the aged-reasonable pensions for the aged.
I have for long been of the opinion that any legislation that is produced that has an economic content should be considered at least high on a level of priorities with the development of a more egalitarian society. I think most of us agree with that today. At least we pay lip service to it. It seems to me this pension plan is a case in point, and that the government is missing a bet in its very careful and cautious approach to the possibilities of this plan.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I have come to the conclusion that this plan is, or should be, very

closely linked with three other pieces of projected legislation the government is presenting to parliament. It seems to me that it is, or should be, concerned with the very problems we have been wrestling with in our banking and commerce committee of late when dealing with the minister's bill with regard to insurance and trust companies.
Here we are dealing with legislation that is designed in some way to offset some of the more socially objectionable features of our present private insurance industry. We are going to great lengths and taking a great deal of time in developing very complicated formulae in order to deal with the private handling of public savings in Canada because that, after all, is what the insurance industry is all about. It is the private handling of public savings.
The bill before us now deals in a very modest way with the public handling of public savings, and I was puzzled a few minutes ago to notice that the minister made a distinction between the funds that flow into private pension plans, or the private insurance industry, and those that will flow into the pension fund authority, a distinction he described as private savings and public savings.
I would suggest this is a really bad-not merely a semantic error-serious misreading of economic facts. I suggest that actually we are dealing in both cases with public savings that in one case fall into irresponsible private hands not responsible to parliament or to the public and which, in the other case, fall into public hands which are controllable by the people's representatives and are responsible to the parliament of the country.
I feel this bill is also, or should be, connected with the legislation regarding the designated areas, this government's attempt-a very praiseworthy attempt-to try and decentralize some of the economic concentrations that have taken place in Canada; its attempt to develop the areas that have been falling behind, and to do so it has adopted legislation which encourages-using both the carrot and stick formula-private enterprise to enter into these areas of the country that have not proven profit making in the past. It has in the case of the maritimes made available a sizeable sum of money from the public treasury to stimulate private development in that area, a measure I heartily support. This also is again dealing with the question of the savings of the Canadian people, how we are going to use them and who is going to have control over their use.
Canada Pension Plan
Then there is another projected piece of legislation which, as I said earlier in the session, I almost hesitate to mention. I see the minister has guessed which one-the moribund Canadian development corporation that apparently has been put into the morgue, or somewhere, to preserve it for the time being.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: It is left in "Troubled Canada."

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Yes, that is right, it is left there. R.I.P.
I suggest that had the government presented some comprehensive legislation dealing with all of these various aspects of handling the savings of the Canadian people we might be moving more rapidly towards the development of what I have suggested earlier should be our goal in a country such as Canada, a more egalitarian society.
I have been contrasting this plan presented to us-and I must admit presented by the minister in a way which will assuage all the fears and anxieties of those who fear any incursions into the preserves of the acquisitive society of today-with some other plans, in particular the Swedish plan. One of the most striking contrasts is that in the first place the Swedes consider the principle of extracting the money from those who can best afford it is a good one to follow, and in Sweden all contributions are paid by the employers. The employers pay the employees' contributions, and in 1960 this amounted to 1.9 per cent of the earned income of an employee. This year it has risen to 4.5 per cent and it is anticipated that legislation will be introduced shortly which will finally set the limits of these contributions up to a probable limit of 10 per cent.
By the end of this year the fund in Sweden will have grown to the level of some 7,500 million krona, which is about $18 million and, if I may, Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote from a report by Mr. Ernst Michanek, who is under secretary of state for the minister for social affairs, labour and housing in Sweden. It is a report issued this year and in it Mr. Michanek says this:
The fund will continue to grow during the initial two or three decades of its operation, but the pace of this growth will gradually decline as the number of pensioners and the amounts of benefits increase.
The decision to build up a huge fund was prompted by the need for making up for the decrease in private savings and private pension funds which was an anticipated effect of the adoption of the new pension system.
The investment of this fund is, to my mind, a very interesting factor to be considered too.

Canada Pension Plan
A maximum of one half the total of premiums received by the pensions found in any calendar year will be made available for loans-amortizable in ten years-to those having paid premiums, if their premiums amount to certain minima. The remaining revenue (premiums and yield) not required for the payment of benefits will be invested in public and private bonds.
Not long ago an article appeared in the London Economist dealing with the Swedish fund in which it stated that at present, already far sooner than the Swedes expected, this fund now has in its control some 45 per cent of all the investment capital of Sweden. As a consequence, the Swedish authorities have been able to organize the economy in a much more direct way than was possible at an earlier stage. This is where the present government is exhibiting the usual Liberal party hesitancy, the usual combination of lofty aims and pedestrian methods which always results in those lofty aims not being reached; their wagons are not hitched to stars, or even to treetops and consequently they usually remain on the ground. The minister himself has observed this on a number of occasions.
I believe this plan should have had two, or perhaps three objectives. As an old man myself I can agree with the minister that I am interested in the care of the aged. But as an ancestor I am interested in the sort of Canada in which my numerous descendants will live. I would not say I am more interested, but I am at least equally interested in the latter aspect of our affairs. Here we have a golden opportunity to begin that direction of the economy to which the present government has paid lip service ever since it came into office. Members will recall the establishment of the economic council of Canada which was to play an important part in directing the economy of this country. Silence has been the only answer from that council to date; we have been told it has been too busy setting its house in order to undertake any housekeeping. Always this government has fallen short of placing in its own hands the power to take any decisive step toward the economic direction of the country. Here in this pension plan there was an opportunity to provide the government with funds which could have been channelled into the Canadian development corporation, if it is not completely dead -funds which could have been used to carry out some of the aims which the minister has attempted to achieve on three or four occasions. One of these I mentioned earlier-the attempt to deal with the problem raised by foreign ownership. Here was another opportunity missed by the minister and by this

government to take some real, decisive action in order to regain some control over our own economy. Here was an opportunity to pool the savings of the Canadian people in very large measure in public hands and, having done so, to devise a weapon by which this increasing and continuing expansion of foreign ownership might have been reversed.
There is another purpose which I think the plan should have had in mind. I have been thinking of it constantly while we have been struggling ineffectually with this ineffectual piece of legislation designed to overcome some of the dangers which arise when privately owned financial institutions control the savings of the Canadian people. It does seem to me that this pension plan should have been the first step toward a public insurance scheme for Canada which would in the end remove most of the care for this type of savings from private to public hands. But the government has been careful in this regard to assure those who have made a handsome profit out of caring for the savings of the Canadian people that they will be allowed to continue to control the vast bulk of those savings.
There is another aspect of the present plan which I find disturbing, namely the provision whereby the provinces of Canada are to have complete access to all the funds which will be accumulated. The minister has mentioned certain areas in which he thinks the savings of the Canadian people should be channelled and no one will quarrel with him about the fields of investment he mentioned. Certainly, they should be channelled into the building of schools, hospitals, and roads-I think those were the undertakings coming within the jurisdiction of provincial legislatures which he mentioned-and certainly the provinces should have access to a proportion of the funds which will be accumulated under this plan. However, I suggest that the development of our economy and the direction in which this development takes place are of equal importance. I believe we shall have to do very much more with regard to the encouragement of development in those areas of Canada which have been lagging behind the more prosperous sectors. I think anyone who has observed the direction of economic development in Canada

and it does not differ to any degree from the trend in other industrialized countries-must have been disturbed by the manner in which greater and greater concentration of industrial potential and financial strength has been flowing into a few restricted areas, leaving a large part of the country to wither, as it were, on the vine.

It is true that the government has been making some praiseworthy, even if ineffectual, attempts to cope with this situation and reverse the trend through legislation designed to benefit designated areas, and through financial aid to the Atlantic provinces. It does seem to me that here is an opportunity to do something decisive in this regard. This will not be an inexpensive project; we shall not do it on the basis of a handout of $100 million to the Atlantic provinces to last them for an indefinite period. We shall require a continuing flow of public investment into these areas. I do not think any of us have any illusions that we can coax private enterprise into unprofitable areas successfully. Some industries will come, of course, as long as there are benefits to be derived from public contributions in the form of exemption from taxation, depreciation allowances, and so on. But in the end we shall have to wrench our economy away from these areas of concentration into these poorly developed areas, and this will take a very large part of the savings of the Canadian people.
The bill before us does not propose to do anything very much in this direction. In the first place, it does not propose to take any sizeable part of the savings of the Canadian people. The minister himself has been at pains to suggest it will not do so. I maintain the plan should have aimed to do just that. It should have aimed to control the majority of the savings of the Canadian people.
Moreover, and I think this is another of the failures of this legislation, we have apparently abandoned the idea of placing the burden of this scheme on the shoulders of those who have the best ability to pay. We are limiting it to $5,000. I see no reason why income above $5,000 should not be taxed for this purpose. I see no reason why we should ask those in the lower income brackets to help finance the old age of those in their own income brackets. This is what I call sharing poverty and I thought our goal was sharing wealth, at least to some degree. Again there is a failure to move toward an egalitarian society and I am at a loss to understand why this government thinks there is anything commendable in placing the whole burden upon those who are least able to bear it while exempting those who are best able to pay.
If there is a case to be made-and I think there is; the case the minister made this afternoon-for those who are now gainfully employed contributing to the welfare of those who have passed that period of their lives
Canada Pension Plan
when they could be gainfully employed, there is an even stronger case to be made for obliging those who have benefited most from our society to contribute to the welfare of those who have benefited least. We observe this principle at least to a limited degree in our income tax legislation. There are, of course, other pieces of legislation in which it is not observed. The old age security regulations provide one example, with their limit of $60. It has always struck me as a scandalous thing that we should limit income in this way.

My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) assures me it is now $120. I might have known that this government would extend it to $120-a full $10 a month. I still do not understand why this government finds it necessary to be so assiduous in its care of the more fortunate members of society while insisting that the less fortunate should be left to finance each other. I believe the Salvation Army have a little saying which they like to bring out at Christmas when they are collecting money- "Its the poor wot 'elps the poor." The government thinks this is a sound principle on which to proceed. It does happen to be a fact of life that those who are less fortunate in their portion of the world's goods are usually more generous about sharing it. But I do not think this government should take advantage of this.
I think, on the other hand, the government should be prepared to place the burden where it should be placed, namely on the more fortunate members of society. I am not for a moment suggesting that those in the lower income brackets should not make their contributions; but I see no reason whatever why this government should not be prepared to build up a really effective fund of the savings of the Canadian people by imposing a large part of the burden on those in the best position to shoulder that burden and to move then toward that transformation of society in the form of an egalitarian society about which the Liberal party is so very voluble when it is not in office. The members of the Liberal party have always assured us that their party is clutching to its bosom this same principle that some of the rest of us have, but they forget about it once they get into office. They say, "We shall not upset the foundations of our acquisitive society but shall, on the contrary, reinforce it by making

Canada Pension Plan
sure that those who are not so fortunate in their lives within this acquisitive society will have enough to keep them alive". I am not satisfied with that. I am not satisfied with anything that reinforces what I consider to be a profoundly immoral and a profoundly unworkable form of society and economy. But I do not hope for anything better from the Liberal party. I was naive enough to hope that the minister might perhaps break ranks, because I know he has professed more advanced views than some of his colleagues; but this afternoon I must confess I was more impressed with his timidity and caution than with his liberalism and progressive ideas. I hope that before this bill comes out of committee some of these shortcomings may be remedied, but it is a faint hope, I suspect.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this stage of the debate, after some very fine contributions by members on both sides of the house, speeches by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh), the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson), and the speech we have just heard this afternoon by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) dealing with the economic implications of the Canada pension plan, it is not easy to say much that has not already been said. I do, however, wish to comment on a few of the general principles involved and make a few points which perhaps may add a little to the debate.
The Canada pension plan, as has been said, is truly a milestone in the development of Canada's social security programs. The Minister of Finance this afternoon reviewed the background of pensions from 1927 to the present measure, and in the debate in this house yesterday the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) indicated the development of pension in terms of general concepts which he outlined as, first the acceptance of public pensions as a public responsibility in 1927, the development of universality in 1952, and he then added the further concept of adequacy of pension plans. I would like to say a few words in the latter part of my remarks about the hon. member's discussion of adequacy and the problems which are involved in arriving at and applying this principle. In the beginning, Mr. Speaker, I think it is clear why we have to adopt the principle of a pension plan which is related to earnings. I was surprised to hear some things from certain members of the house, such as the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. McCutcheon), who said as reported at page 9916 of Hansard:

I suggest the self-employed and the farm people would be much better off under a modernized, up to date flat rate plan.
It is very easy to advocate this when you are not in a position to implement it. The government must bear the financial responsibility of these measures. Using a flat rate plan to achieve adequacy is, first, very very costly. No one is more aware of that, of course, than the Minister of Finance, with his strenuous efforts to improve our budgetary situation. The second reason why the flat rate benefit cannot be used for this purpose is outlined very well in the white paper which was placed before this house; it is simply that the same dollars do not mean the same things in different parts of the country. Seventy five dollars in the city of Vancouver, metropolitan Toronto or metropolitan Montreal is not the same thing as $75 in some of the Atlantic provinces or some of the smaller rural areas where the cost of living is different. The only way one can cope with the problem of different needs in different parts of the country, related to the very complex problem of what is the standard of living we are talking about, is to provide a plan which has some adjustment features in it. This plan has some of these adjustment features in it, and I think it combines them very well.
The second point I would like to make is in regard to actuarial studies. I was disturbed at the remarks of the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith) when I read them in Hansard, and perhaps I have misinterpreted them. In Hansard of last night, as reported at page 10125, the hon. member is reported as having said:
I hope she-
The hon. member was referring to the Minister of National Health and Welfare:
-will tell us whether or not this report was drawn up by the chief actuary of the department of insurance alone or whether there were outside actuaries, or others, involved.
Apparently the hon. member for Perth places a great deal of importance-if I have interpreted him correctly-on whether or not outside actuaries were used in this connection. I hope I am not doing him an injustice, because I had the privilege of serving as a civil servant when he was a minister and I know that his relationship with the civil service was admirable and strictly correct. Therefore I hope this is not a reflection on the actuaries of the department of insurance.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, I can assure the hon. member

now that this was not so. I meant to congratulate the minister on using the government's actuaries.

speechtext:
I appreciate that the hon. member has set the record straight, Mr. Speaker, because I think it is possible of being misinterpreted the way it is reported in Hansard. But even when we have dealt with the question of the actuaries' report- and in many circles a great deal of importance has been placed on the actuaries' report-I think we have to bear in mind the comments made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare in her remarks of last night. An actuarial report cannot mean the same thing when dealing with public plans as it means when dealing with the private insurance industry. When an actuary makes his studies for a private insurance company he has to deal with two basic assumptions, the expectation of life-and here it is not as mathematically precise as one might expect; life expectancy is increasing, which is a very fine thing-and the second is the interest on the money invested. The actuary has to make assumptions in these respects. These are assumptions of a very broad, general nature. But within this scope the actuary can apply his technique and training in a way which leads to a fair degree of precision.
But look at the additional assumptions that have to be involved when you deal with a public plan. The minister pointed out that the basic and variable assumption is the question of the level of earnings on which the contribution is going to be raised. This first involves the question of the number of people who are going to be employed and assumptions with regard to the rate of unemployment. It involves the natural growth of the labour force; and when we start looking at the natural growth of the labour force we are dealing with things which are not predictable according to the generally accepted techniques of actuaries. We have to think of immigration to this country, which is a great deal; we have to think of birth rates, which are generally remarkably variable and are not predictable. Then we have to think of the attitudes toward employment. These attitudes are reflected in the approach to the retirement age. I am not at all sure that the desire of everyone in the future will be to retire from active employment at as early an age as possible, for reasons of self-satisfaction, pride and self-respect itself. Many people choose to be employed as long as they are physically and mentally able to be employed. It may be that with an increase in the 20220-644
Canada Pension Plan
expectancy of life we may see a different approach to the whole question of the retirement age, which will in turn affect the number of people who will be employed. Then we think of the number of married women who go back into the labour force after their children reach a certain age. All these factors will influence the number of people involved and the payrolls affected by the pension rates. They are not predictable in any conventional sense.
The minister again pointed out the problem of prediction of prices and price changes, and on top of that productivity changes. All of these are involved in projections of rates of growth of funds in future years. They are not predictable financially in any greater sense than they are predictable by an economist, a statistician, or a large number of other people trained to deal with these matters; as a result we get a wide spread at the high and low of the fund. But that is no reflection on anyone; it is merely a reflection of the great difficulty of making any estimate of the growth of the fund in which we could place the confidence we should like to place in dealing with these matters.
The third point I should like to make deals with the integration of private plans. Again I am disturbed by the remarks of the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard) as reported at page 9909 of Hansard, when he said:
Many people are wondering what is going to happen to the amounts already invested in private companies. What assurance will they have that they will not go bankrupt now that they are losing that income? None, actually. What assurance will they have that those company pension funds will not be nationalized by governments? There again, absolutely none.
I disagree, Mr. Speaker, completely with that kind of remark, which I consider to be irresponsible and the kind of thing which should not be said by people in public life. The white paper which was laid before us makes it abundantly clear at page 22 that the Canada pension plan will not take over and absorb reserves which have been built up by private pension plans.
There is a problem of integration. I thought the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) was going to deal with the problem of the integration of plans for the benefit of public servants under the Public Service Superannuation Act with the Canada pension plan, but I am informed that his parliamentary secretary may deal with it. But from looking at the existing scheme it is quite clear that this plan will permit an improvement in

Canada Pension Plan
benefits under private plans for the same level of premium, or a reduction in premium for the same level of benefit, or possibly a little of both. The Canada pension plan is a better deal, dollar for dollar, than the existing plan. I should like to say, through you, Mr. Speaker, to all public servants both in Ottawa and in Canada that the reports which have been appearing in the press to the effect that public servants will be adversely affected by the Canada pension plan are completely without foundation. This plan will permit a degree of integration to their benefit either through reduced premiums, increased benefits, or possibly both. Because the Canada pension plan is that much better value dollar for dollar.
The question of integration of existing schemes has to be worked out plan by plan. They will have to be negotiated by management and unions, and a decision must be made whether or not they simply want to add the Canada pension plan or whether or not a component will be substituted. This plan is a good plan, one which offers benefits which are very generous compared with the benefits offered by private insurance.
By the same token there is a great role for private insurance in this country, and there will continue to be so. In 1950 when a joint committee of this house and the other place met to consider the problem of the old age security plan which was eventually evolved, representations were made to the effect that this step would prove very harmful to the insurance industry. But the reverse was the case. The effect of the old age security plan which was implemented in 1952 was to make people more pension conscious than they ever were before. It increased the sale of life insurance and made more people aware of the need for planning a retirement income on an adequate scale. I am confident that this will again be the case. We have not yet approached adequacy; nor can we approach it on the scale we should like in view of the standard of living many Canadians have built up for themselves. It reminds me of the old story that a man's reach must exceed his grasp; else what is a heaven for? Obviously we must strive for a higher and higher standard of living. As we achieve more we want more, and that will always be the case.
It will be the job of the private insurance industry continuously to add extra supplements to the public plan, which is merely the floor. These supplements provided by private insurance will be in terms of individual requirements and resources and will be tailor

made. I confidently make the prediction that the effect of this plan will be to make people even more insurance conscious. It will not be harmful to the industry but will provide the base which will be much more defensible in terms of all sections of the community; and from this the private insurance industry will benefit.
The last point I want to make is in connection with adjustments to the plan. I was a little disturbed by some remarks made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles)-I cannot find his exact words in Hansard at the moment-to the effect that $10 a month was old hat and that we will have to do very much better than that now. He also said that the adjustment made a year ago does not amount to anything now and that adjustments must continually be made. Let us look at the adjustments which are built into this plan. First of all there is the cost of living adjustment. It is true that this is limited to 2 per cent in any one year and it is not possible to implement it before 1968. The second adjustment is based on the earnings index. The minimum $600 and maximum $5,000 are adjustable according to the formula as earnings adjust. Earnings themselves will slide up as the general productivity of the economy advances.
I do not think that the hon. members who are complaining about the lack of flexibility in making adjustments to future pensions are so much worried about the Canada pension plan; they keep coming back to the old age security component of it. Nevertheless, I come back again to this point, that it is the responsibility of the government in power and the responsibility of this parliament to guarantee not only a basic dollar and a basic pension but also the integrity of the dollar and the integrity of the pension. That is the greatest contribution which any government could make. If pension increases are followed by massive deficits year after year at the height of the cycle as well as at the low points of the cycle, which in turn leads to inflation, then we are not serving our old age pensioners or anybody else well. Fiscal responsibility has to be the core of the guarantee of the actual worth of the pension dollar.
It is very easy to say, Mr. Speaker, that adjustments should be made to the old age security pension and that perhaps it would be possible to vote the necessary dollars and to run up further deficits. But we all know the consequences of continuous massive deficits without regard to the business cycle. When times are bad or in times of recession

there are very few in this house who would not believe it proper to run up deficits on a large scale. But I would argue that very few of us would be prepared to say that deficits should be run up on a massive scale regardless of the high point or the low point of the business cycle. That would be irresponsible and would lead to inflation.
Pension adjustments have to be related to the state of the economy and to productivity. Hon. members who argue for pension adjustments have offered no criterion for automatic productivity adjustments because such criterion is not easily found; but within the Canada pension plan I submit that there are built-in adjustments. It is true they are limited but they are better than those which have been devised so far.
Within the old age security component we have a cost of living adjustment. I for one hope the cost of living adjustment provision never has to operate, because if it does not a stable dollar will make a greater contribution than an inflated dollar, which will mean that the cost of living provision will not have to be used.
I am also confident that over a period of years there will be an orderly, responsible review in terms of the productivity of Canada's economy. This and this alone must be the final guarantee of what we can do. If we do not create conditions for growth, if we do not create conditions for a high level of employment, if we do not create conditions under which expanding incomes are possible, then the rest is not possible.

Mr. Speaker, I have spoken before in the house on the pension plan, but it was on the earlier plans introduced and at the time I spoke I expressed a note of caution and said that I was quite unhappy about some of the deficiencies in the other plans. I am very happy this afternoon that the plan we now have before us contains provisions for dependant children, widows, disabled persons and so on.
We in the opposition have been quite conscious for some time that any time we have criticized the government it has been called obstruction. I am not sure how successful the Liberals have been in selling this idea, but this is certainly the echo we see in the newspapers every day. Therefore I think it is only fair for me to say now that if it were not for such obstruction we might have been saddled with that first plan which the minister introduced so proudly, so politically and so long ago.

speechtext: Three maple leaves, too.
