speechtext:
In fact, we might even have been saddled with the second plan. I am not suggesting this plan is perfect but certainly it is a great improvement. I think it is basically a very good plan and I hope we will be able to work very hard on it in the committee stage and make a few more improvements.
I thought the remarks of the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) were quite valid. I am not convinced that the only thing we should talk about at this point is whether the plan is desirable because that would leave us with no debate at all, but he did mention that the committee would need a considerable amount of time. The bill is very large and complex. There are not many members of the house who are trained or equipped to deal with all aspects and phases of it, but I do think that most members are quite familiar with the effects of certain sections. They are very familiar with the needs of certain parts of the population. I am sure that all members are most interested in the bill, so the fact is that we will need to do a great amount of work on it.
I do not believe any time limit should be suggested. I would hate to think we would have to start all over again if this session should be prorogued. Therefore I hope that something will be worked out in order that the committee can look into the bill thoroughly and completely, so that its work

Canada Pension Plan
will result in solid progress which will not be lost but which will be carried forward into the next session.
I followed with considerable attention the remarks of the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron). I was particularly impressed by his remarks about the fund that would be accumulated and the use that the state could make of this money in directing the economy of the nation. I am sure most of us realize that in today's world the governments of most countries have been directing the economies of their nations more and more. Some go about it to a greater extent than others and different methods are used.
The only point on which I can agree with the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands to any extent is that I am not sure I want to see these funds in the hands of the provinces rather than in the hands of the federal government. I think we all agree it is a good thing that the provinces through this fund will have additional moneys available that can be lent to municipalities for various purposes, but I do think we are missing the boat a little by putting these funds into the hands of the provinces from which they are raised.
We have seen over the last few years that the biggest and richest provinces are not necessarily those that need the most help, and if the vast amounts accumulated in this fund go straight back to the provinces whence the money came it will do nothing to help the have-not provinces and will deprive the federal government of an opportunity to use these funds or part of them to provide extra assistance in those provinces where additional assistance is so obviously needed at the present time.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands referred to the Canada development fund as proposed by the Liberal party in the last election campaign. In fact, several members have mentioned it but the emphasis of their references has been more on its absence. I am not sure that any Liberal spokesman has explained why what was so good at election time is so repugnant now, but I suppose if we were to ask them to explain all those things that were so good at election time which they have failed to do they would hardly be talking about anything else in the house.
While I have said I have some reservation about the advisability of turning the funds over to the provinces, and while I think the federal government is missing a chance to even up the needs of the provinces, I have

never been too sold on the general idea of the federal government amassing a fund of money which it can use for investment purposes to direct or assist the economy. It has always been my belief that, rather than encouraging our people to save more money by putting it into the hands of the federal government to lend, our people should be encouraged to invest more of their money. Canadians are the most cautious investors in the world. They are also the most consistent savers. Therefore if we are to retain more of the profits of industries within this country I think the Canadian people, rather than just receiving interest on loans, should be persuaded to engage more in risk investment, that is, in the share capital of companies.
The question of the provinces building up funds and having control of them is not my only reservation with regard to the present plan. If the province of Quebec has the same plan as the federal government, frankly I am unable to understand why that province wants to operate its own plan. I am unable to understand why any other province would want to set up a plan essentially the same and to opt out of the federal plan. I have never believed in this opting out process at all. If something is good for the country, I do not think one Canadian is that much different from another and I think it should be quite possible to so arrange the plan that it will be generally suitable throughout the country, and once we have it in that form it should then be a federal scheme, not a partly federal scheme which applies to only nine provinces now, which next year may only apply to eight and the following year may only apply to half a dozen.
There is another point about which I am somewhat puzzled, although perhaps further study of the bill will clear it up. When there is this opting out principle and when the province of Quebec has its own scheme, I cannot understand how the federal pension plan can be truly portable. Certainly, if a province opts out, the only logical reason I can think of for its preferring to run its own scheme is that there is some difference in its scheme as compared with the federal plan. If they already have control of the fund and they want to opt out, there must be that difference, and that difference is a very significant one. If the difference is a significant one, then those Canadians who are going from province to province will have to accept the significant difference in their pension plan. How can we then call the plan a portable plan? If these differences are insig-

nificant or likely to be, then I am left all the more puzzled as to why any province wants to run its own plan. I would dearly love to have that explained.
I was happy to hear the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) say he felt the Dominion of Canada could afford this plan. I am sure there has been nothing in his budgets to date to indicate that the government has found any way to manage the financial affairs of this nation in such a way as to get rid of deficits. We are aware, of course, that while they have followed the general economic policies practised by the previous government, the full effect of those policies has meant comparatively good times. The gross national product is up. We can therefore expect a much higher return from some taxes. However, the note of optimism from the minister was almost as surprising as it was welcome. I found it a little surprising when the minister stated that the revenues from income taxes alone received by the federal government, once this plan gets into operation, will drop by about $100 million. I hope I understood him correctly. I had no idea it would be that amount. Certainly, we must all bear in mind that this is an extra cost of administration of the scheme. It is costing the federal government $100 million per year at the outset, once this plan goes into operation.
I am sure that with the rising standard of wages, when the scheme is adjusted higher, there will be a similar adjustment in the revenue loss of the federal government through income taxes. This should be calculated as a cost of administration. I am not sure if the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) added this item to administration costs when she spoke of them. I think it is well for us to take a look at it. Perhaps we can examine it more closely in the committee.
I was much impressed by the argument presented by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron). He said he thought this plan did not go far enough. He wanted it to be an all-Canada insurance plan. I am afraid that he is quite socialistic. While I was impressed with his argument, I am afraid that I cannot go as far as he did in adopting that argument. I am happy, however, that there is room for private insurance plans. I believe that individuals have a right to look after themselves if they desire to do so. The duty of the government is to help those who need help rather than force everyone to come under a scheme. There
Canada Pension Plan
are a good many people, even in the low income brackets in this country, who resent the thought they will be accepting a government handout. People look for a plan like this when they have not found it possible to get involved with an employer-employee scheme, or perhaps they have not been able to make financial arrangements to enter a private insurance scheme. The only assistance they really want is a government direction to make it possible for them, in their income group, to get into a scheme or a pension plan for which they can pay. Then, they can say, I am carrying my own load.
Sometimes in today's society we lose track of the human value and benefit there is to individuals who want to be able to say they are standing on their own two feet. This is especially important, I think, when we reflect that so many of us feel that success or adequacy can be measured by the amount of money a person can earn. Even in the lower income brackets, this feeling of adequacy is there. There is much pride in being able to take care of oneself. The extent of the assistance given in this plan, and the form of assistance, is all that is requested by some. I am quite aware of the fact that there are many in the lower income brackets who feel quite a bit different. They feel that those who are rich should pay for everything. There is a constant struggle in this house about that principle. Perhaps the hon. member for Na-naimo-Cowichan-The Islands gave us the best answer to that struggle when he said that we take cognizance of it by means of the Income Tax Act. Certainly if there is a great need to adjust the extent to which the rich shall contribute to government schemes, the Income Tax Act is the one means by which it can be done very fairly.
I hope that when this matter is referred to the committee its work will be arranged so we will not be rushed. I hope the organizations that may feel they will need considerable time to prepare properly a brief to deal with the part of the plan which most interests them will be given a sympathetic hearing, and that there will be a great deal of cooperation between the various groups so that they may present their arguments in an orderly manner. I hope the committee may know from day to day what they are likely to be considering and that they will not have to be sitting day and night, day in and day out in order to meet a deadline. I should like to refer to the flag committee for a moment in that regard. I was not a member of that committee, but I do feel it was asking a little

Canada Pension Plan
too much of the members of the committee to sit so often, day after day, and concentrate to such an extent on that subject. I could certainly understand the feeling of those who wanted to get the matter completed and relieve the pressure on us.
I submit that the same pressures are not present in connection with this matter. When the committee is studying something as complicated as this pension plan, there should be no suggestion of a deadline because that would have only harmful effect on the work that should be done. I do not want to be misinterpreted: I think we all wish to see a pension plan. However, we have had enough experience in the house to know that sometimes we jump a little too quickly, and a second thought or a little assistance from someone might be of great value. I suggest that having waited a long time for this we want to make sure it is as good as we can refine it to be in committee, rather than face the immediate necessity of amendment just as soon as it is passed.

Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to note how the Canada pension plan and the formula which made it possible were established.
On the judicial and constitutional levels, this measure falls under section 92(13) of the British North America Act which gives the provinces exclusive rights over property and civil rights. As Mr. Ollivier clearly pointed out in one of his treatises, a distinction must be established between pure civil rights and social legislation. This distinction, however, was recognized in amendments to the British North America Act, the first of which was in connection with the Unemployment Insurance Act introduced in this country by a Liberal government. Needless to say that this amendment had first been approved by all the provinces just as a similar amendment and a similar agreement by all the provinces have made possible the setting up of a Canada pension plan. It shows also the priority of the provinces in that field, as their consent is required for the establishment of any social legislation, and also the right of the provinces to discuss the matter and lay down conditions.
On the Canadian political level it was necessary to prevent what some people call the "balkanization" of the country. The agreement reached ensures co-ordination between the Quebec plan and the Ottawa plan,

and the pensions will be portable for those who are moving from one province to another. The rates and benefits will be the same throughout Canada, and the danger is avoided.
From the economic standpoint the public reserves accumulated by the federal plan will be made available to the provinces, which will be able to use them for their own purposes: education, highways, the development of their natural resources and other matters of provincial jurisdiction. The source of the right being provincial, it was normal to let the receipts go to the provinces.
There will be two pension plans but their application will be co-ordinated and standardized for the benefit of the Canadian taxpayer who, after all, will pay the shot.
Such is in my opinion the result of a formula which is called co-operative federalism. That formula deserves to be looked into, since it makes possible the achievement of a very important piece of social legislation.
The result is important; it shows that the formula has the required flexibility to meet the present needs and that far from being an exception intended to isolate one or the other of the provinces in the confederative pact, the formula strengthens unity by guaranteeing to all Canadians equal benefits under the pension plan.
What does Quebec ask? The guarantee that it may freely use its constitutional rights. What does Quebec do? It co-operates; here, it reveals the details of its pension plan which, after being studied in comparison with the federal scheme, enrich both plans. Who benefits from this co-operation? The Canadian taxpayer wherever he lives.
The Quebec people are not street fighters. They are moderate, peaceful and they hate disorder. In Quebec city they did not turn their backs on the Queen, but on terrorism. If the Leader of the Opposition would only stop blaming the province of Quebec and the Quebec members of the federal cabinet and work in the general interest, he would find more co-operation not only in the province of Quebec but also among the French Canadian members of his own party and among the English Canadians who still have some objectivity.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us a pension bill which is the third one introduced by the government and, in opposition to what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) said, may I point out that we on this side of the house are not neglectful of our old people. In fact we hope this bill, after being properly tailored, will fit the need.
Canada Pension Plan
As it stands I do not believe it will fit the need, and after making a few criticisms I shall try to show in a positive way what we should do about it. It is an old trick, to claim that the opposition has no consideration for old people; but if one looks at the record of social justice and at the record of performance by the previous administration it will be seen great steps were taken during the period of that administration to improve not only the conditions of old people but to solve problems of social justice in all fields.
At this stage of the bill it is necessary to talk principles, and it is difficult to do that without going over the history of some past mistakes. I for one think our present old age pension scheme is one of the best in the world. I do not think we are far behind most countries of the western world, free enterprise countries, in looking after our old people. Of course I am not satisfied to leave it there. We must not rest on our laurels. I do not think many people can live on $75 a month. But as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) has said, it is the basic thing which concerns us and I think it would be as well for us to confine the compulsory part of the plan to this very matter. It would be a strange thing indeed if in a free enterprise country such as Canada-and I hope and pray it will always remain such-we should provide any compulsory system of old age retirement benefits designed to give people what I would call a luxury standard of living. On the other hand I do not want to see any segment of our population left without provision for meeting their basic needs.
As I see this bill, it will not bring a great deal of benefit to those who do not already have a considerable measure of security. Coverage is supposed to be universal I am sure we would all like to see this brought about, but are we likely to get it under the terms of the present bill? It appears to me that after agricultural labourers, all those employed in lumbering, fishing, horticulture, and those who are handicapped or disabled for one reason or another have been excluded, a large section of our population will not be protected. My feeling is we should retain the principles of our present system of old age benefits, a system which includes everybody regardless of income or occupation.
The basic rate is, in my opinion, still not high enough. At the present time a single person cannot possibly get along on less than $100 a month and a married couple might need double that sum, or possibly $175 a month.

Canada Pension Plan
It would be easy to get into an argument about where the money is to come from. Well, it can only come from the earning power of our people, from the gross national product. I do not wish to become involved in a long discussion about whether it is better to take the money out of our left hand pocket or from our right hand pocket or whether we should take it from the employer or from the employee. It all comes from the same source, the ability of the Canadian people to create wealth. If we end up providing $300 a month, somebody will have to pay for it; if we provide such a pension for everybody beyond a certain age it means we are asking those who are presently working, the youth of the country, to pay the shot.
There are features of the bill which I like. I like the recognition that we cannot jump into this scheme right away. I like the recognition that it will take time to build up a fund capable of meeting payments of the kind proposed. But I am not in favour of a system which would place all the burden on the young people who are actually producing the wealth. We should take a good look at this plan to make sure we are not setting up a pension scheme which will be badly broken almost as soon as it comes into operation.
It has been suggested that once the fund has been built up we shall be able to lend all the money to the provinces. I am not at all sure that there will be a large enough fund even to meet its commitments, let alone have hundreds of millions left over to lend to the provinces. We all feel strongly about looking after our old people but I feel strongly, too, about looking after our young people, those who are presently wage earners. If this is to be really a national scheme I would be more in favour of the compulsory portion of the bill. In a democracy we are all in it together, I suppose; we are all paying equally according to our means. This at least is fair. But it does not seem to me that this bill will be fair. It seems to me that a great many people will have to pay very heavily for the privilege of retiring in comfort, while others will get something like a bonanza. It has been my experience that bonanzas do not come easily; somebody has to pay for them. We must make sure that in seeking to look after our old age we who are closer to retirement do not place an unnecessary burden on those who are now in the most active and productive stage of their lives.

Personally, after I was married and had the responsibility of raising a family, the security I wanted was in the years when the family was young. The whole idea of saving seems to me to be getting out of line. We are obsessed with the idea that we should all retire at the age of 70 with $300 or $400 a month. I suggest this is almost sad. If a man has lived all his working life and has never had a real opportunity to give his family and children the things he wanted to give them, there is something almost sad in retirement on a pension of $300 or $400 when it is too late.
I am against compulsion in all its aspects. I would accept compulsion only if I was sure it would lead to a better system of security than any scheme I could work out on my own. I am one who thinks it is inefficient to expect the government to do our planning and saving for us. It has been said that private industry is incapable of handling retirement funds. I think some of the plans which private industry has produced are both efficient and generous. I would much prefer to see the companies themselves putting attractive retirement plans in operation and making sure that government interference is unnecessary, rather than that they should be placed under compulsion in any way. I should like to see the government tailor this bill so as to make its provisions available to everybody and so attractive that we would all be glad to participate, even management.
I get tired of hearing the same old wail from the far left to the effect that those who can pay should pay. This assumes we can carry on this Robin Hood type of taxation forever. I suggest there are not enough rich people in Canada to pay this whole shot. Those who are very well off are already paying enormous amounts out of their hard earned incomes in support of all kinds of social legislation, and some of it is wasted. I am in favour of giving help to those who need it but I am not in favour of killing the goose that lays the golden eggs. Whenever our socialist friends wish to prove that socialism is a good thing they point to the example of Sweden. They tell us everything is rosy there. But no one emigrates from Canada to Sweden-the flow is all the other way. Most of us in Canada, the pioneer type, came out here because we wanted the right to enjoy the fruits of our labour. We wanted to own property. We wanted, if you like, to have the right to gamble. We gamble with our lives every day. Others gamble with their money by putting it into investments. I do not think

they should be chased down the road for ever and amen, and robbed.
This Robin Hood type of government is very appealing. It is particularly appealing when one does not have the responsibility for producing the money or even for taking it from the people who have it. Socialism will not work in Canada; but social justice does work and has worked. Our present old age pension has relieved the minds of thousands and thousands of people and given them a modicum of security which they never enjoyed before. I think we should continue our old age pension system very much as it has been in the past, with this exception-that we should raise it. Then having raised it perhaps a little more to make sure there is no distress amongst our old people, our younger people should be encouraged to save money on their own. They should be given a really comprehensive plan, and where industries are already heavily taxed in contributing these funds perhaps we could bring in a system whereby we could amalgamate all our pension plans and simplify the whole procedure.
I do not think complete control of our industry, our pensions and everything else will work as well as properly organized free enterprise. I do not think that a compulsory system of making our young people save is half as good as encouraging them to get out and earn, and then save in a sensible plan of their own choosing. At least they should have the choice of opting out. If we allow one province to opt out it means we are not enforcing our democratic will on minorities; and I for one look upon this question as dealing with a minority of one. Every individual person in Canada must, in my opinion, be allowed to retain some of his freedom of movement, and I resent being told that I have no ability to look after my own affairs, and that I must bow to a paternal form of government.

Mr. Speaker, I will relate my remarks to the bill before us, and I would ask the co-operation of people opposite in relating their questions to the bill, if they wish to ask any. This is supposed to be a universal bill; one for all Canadians. My criticism of it is very plain, namely that it leaves out a vast number of Canadians who I think should benefit under the bill-those who need it the most. I do not know what is going to happen to those people who have not been mentioned in the bill and are considered as having automatically opted out due to the industry in which they happen to be engaged. Apparently they are not going to be able to have the full benefit of the bill.
What about the self-employed people of Canada, of whom there are still a great number and of whom, I might repeat, I hope there will always be a great number? I refer to those people who own their own small farms or their own small businesses. What kind of a deal does this bill as presented give to these people? I am not a Philadelphia lawyer, but as I read the bill, it offers them a chance to benefit under the bill at double the cost of other people; and incidentally, in a great many cases it means they will start at the age of 18, perhaps, and pay for 30 or 40 years at a double rate. This does not seem equitable to me. I think this is something we should look at, not only in this house but in com-

mittee. Let us make it a universal bill and have it apply equally to every citizen of Canada. If there is a compulsive part in it- and I think there are times when you must have compulsion-let us have the compulsion equally distributed amongst everybody.
With regard to portability, Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see that the bill at least purports to say that this plan will be completely portable and you will be able to receive your pension if you move from one job to another in no matter what part of Canada. I think this is fair to everybody and I do not know why anybody would want to opt out. Nobody wants to opt out if it is perfectly fair to everybody. What is the benefit in having a special scheme for one province or another? Why not act like a nation for the people in this great Canada, all under one flag, all with equal rights, and with the priming pumps in every province making sure we get a full flow of water. Why allow a particular section to opt out? If you must be compulsive, be compulsive and put us all over the same block.
It is not good enough to say, "Let us make it universal; let us make it portable''. It has to be practical. How are we going to pay for it? I suggest we should take a good look at this aspect of the question, because this afternoon the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) said he is not at all sure that ten years from now we are going to be able to afford this plan. If in the end, after all the argument has been made, we do think that there is something to be gained here by the people of Canada as individuals as well as collectively, then we will vote for this measure. So let hon. members opposite not bother to put up any straw men or to put words in our mouths by saying we are criticizing this or that, until they hear what the critics say. Why should the Minister of Finance put words in our mouths? This debate is still young and I think that even some of the points I have made have some validity. The plan is not universal. As far as equity is concerned we do want it to be equitable in addition to universal, portable and practical. It is very practical to tax the so-called rich. Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of attention, though possibly with less interest, to the speakers from the official opposition on this bill, but to me at least their arguments were not particularly persuasive. Before I proceed further I should like to assure the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Bigg) that this speech is my own and was not written by any of the backroom boys. It is my own opinion. It is as I feel.
As a Canadian and as a Newfoundlander I am happy to support this legislation. As a member of parliament I am as proud to be a member of the party which has presented it as I will be of the government which makes it law. Representing a district in one of the larger provinces of this country, New-foundland-Labrador, one of the richer provinces in everything but money, I can easily see the effect which this complex bill will have on the people I have the honour to represent, many of whom now suffer from substandard incomes. This situation is changing, but not quickly enough for those of us who are in a hurry.
I am not an economist, Mr. Speaker. Yet I have had the basic test applied to me, the test of meeting a weekly payroll, and that for a good many years. This is a test which I suggest might be applied to some of our theoretical economists. The reason I support the bill is that I believe it will provide for a nation-wide system of social insurance for every Canadian no matter where he may live, whatever his circumstances may be, whatever moves he may make, and whatever economic changes may occur.
Before coming to Ottawa I lived very near a home for the aged and infirm which is operated by the Sisters of Mercy. It is a model for all homes of its type. We have many others, of course, in St. John's. There is a home which is very well operated by the Salvation Army and also one operated by the

United Church. There are others as well and they are all excellently run, but because I lived near this home I had occasion to visit there often. While this home was run perfectly, while the guests had every attention and care, I found that so many of them were unhappy. I sensed that basically there was a sense of loneliness, of uselessness, but above all a sense of insecurity. They simply did not have enough money.
I remember one old gentleman saying to me: "You know, the tragedy of old age is not that one is old but that one is young". I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that you and all other members of the house know many people with young minds imprisoned in aging bodies. Some of us have some security. There are others, far too many, who have none. There are many who listen, wait, eat, sleep and dream. Time is relentlessly pursuing these people. In a few years someone younger will take their jobs or possibly a machine will replace them. What will retirement mean to them? This legislation means, I suggest, security. It also means dignity and decency for the elderly, the old, the people who have borne the burden of the heat of the day. They are people who deserve our respect and who need our help. That is why I welcome and support Bill No. C-136.
This government has been called many things. It has been called indecisive, ineffective. This can be and should be refuted. The government has tackled courageously many difficult problems. It has solved many and others are in process of solution. I should like to commend warmly our planners, our government and in particular the minister for what I like to think of as their future-mind-edness, their concern for the future of all of us who will one day be old.
The minister and others have explained in detail the background of the bill. May I now for a moment or two attempt to answer some of the questions that I feel Canadians are asking. I know my own constituents are asking these questions: How much will I pay? What will the benefits be? Will there be other benefits? Yes, there will be other benefits. As to the question, how much will I pay, the answer is that the contribution rates will be designed so that the average rate is 1J per cent for both employer and employee at the average level of earnings. In view of the fact that no contribution is made on the first $600 per annum of earnings, this will mean that the contribution rate on earnings from $600 to $5,000 per year will be approximately 1.8 per cent for employer and
Canada Pension Plan
employee. The contribution rate for selfemployed persons will be double that because they must pay both the employer and employee contributions.
The proposed contributory plan will become effective as soon as the constitutional amendment concerning survivor and disability benefits is passed and this legislation is passed by parliament. This will take some time but I am quite sure it will be in effect not later than January 1, 1966. The benefits will amount to approximately 25 per cent of the average adjusted wage. The term "adjusted wage" is used because in calculating the benefits, the wages on which contributions were actually paid will be adjusted upwards as the level of wages rises in the country. Benefits will also be adjusted upwards because of the fact some persons may have had some years of very low income during their period of contribution. In calculating the average wage on which benefits are based, one year of low income may be dropped for every ten years of contribution.
Perhaps at this point I might give some indication of the scale of benefits which will be received under the Canada pension plan. For purposes of comparison, I will use the example of a man or woman whose average salary is $300 per month. His or her retirement pension, payable at the beginning of the third year, will be $15 per month; at the sixth year, $37.50 per month, and at the eleventh year, $75 per month. This is, of course, in addition to the present old age pension of $75, or a total of $150, if there is no further increase made in the present $75 pension.
Now, a great deal has been said about the effect of this plan on other pension plans now in existence. Questions have been raised as to whether this plan would attempt to control the benefits of private plans. Well, the Canada pension plan leaves it entirely to the operators of the private plans to determine whether, and if so to what extent, private plans will be modified. Of course there are many employers who have not yet introduced plans of their own. It is the hope of this government that the Canada pension plan, by providing a basic pension, will also provide encouragement for others to augment it by a supplementary pension plan.
In the case of existing plans, particularly where these plans are not overly generous or the employer may have been considering an improvement in any case, many employers may simply leave them unchanged. This Canada pension plan would, in these cases, simply be added on and so provide a much

Canada Pension Plan
better total pension. Other employers, who know that people are far more important than profits, with adequate pension plans may wish to have the same over-all benefit levels as before, and adjust the contributions to the level required to produce these benefits. In any event, because deductions will not be made from salaries under $600 or over $5,000, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) estimates the plan will cost only 1 per cent of the cost of the payroll. This 1 per cent is also tax deductible.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this Canada pension plan is good, sound, beneficial legislation. As I said before, it is an example of the future-mindedness of our minister and of the government. I warmly support it and urge the earliest possible enactment of it.
The late President Kennedy, soon after assuming office, called a conference on aging. In view of the fact that the aged now form, and will continue to form, an increasingly large part of our population as health standards improve, I suggest some thought should be given to this problem. It is a fact that people over 65 are increasing at a rate of a little over twice that of the national average. I know, of course, the government is keenly aware of this problem, and for this I am happy. I am happy to notice, too, and commend the good work now being done by the Senate committee here on the same subject.
I know, Mr. Speaker, that it is this government's hope that as each of us reaches the time of slowing down it can be done in health, dignity, serenity and security, with the satisfaction of being needed and wanted, of still being a part of our vital society. In a month, a year or perhaps longer, every Canadian will have to leave his job and give it up to someone younger than he is or to an electronic machine. He will then begin his period of retirement. Is he or she sufficiently protected? I am concerned about the 30 per cent approximately of our people who already have protection, but I am far more concerned about the vast majority who have not. Are the children protected? The legislation I support today, Mr. Speaker, is the beginning of this security, the beginning of dignity for the aged in Canada. I support it wholeheartedly.

speechtext:
I welcome the opportunity, Mr. Speaker, of saying a few words on the Canada pension plan, just as four days ago I had the pleasure of welcoming the hon. lady minister to Baffin

island where she had taken the time to come to open a new hospital for the Eskimo people. I think I should tell the house that the hon. lady did herself proud on the island. After all, she was before an audience of some 300 Eskimo people who can constitute a unique sort of truth squad, not truth in the sense of whether the words correspond with the facts, but truth in the sense of whether you are sincere or not. I can tell the house that she was well received, because they knew she was busy, they knew she had many other things including this pension plan to prepare for the house. I will welcome her back into the Northwest Territories any time she wants to come, with the exception perhaps of during the next general election campaign.
I wanted to make a few remarks on the Canada pension plan tonight, remarks that put forward essentially my own ideas gathered from ten years of welfare administration prior to entering this house, based on training in the field of welfare and more recently, in the last few years, based on reading, and the first two versions of the Canada pension plan, as well as assorted other opinions I have been able to gather. I shall put forward my own ideas in this case and shall do so as a person representing nearly all the Eskimo people in this country, and many of our Indian people who, after all, have a lot to gain from any system of expanded social security.
I open my remarks by saying that I strongly believe Bill No. C-136 should have been referred to a parliamentary committee prior to second reading. I know this can be done and no doubt hon. members who are as new as I am, who have never been here before the twenty sixth parliament, can think of an instance in which it has been done. I think of this instance particularly because it concerned a bill that would have had the effect of dividing the Northwest Territories into two separate territories. After much discussion in this house and much uncertainty, it was decided by unanimous agreement of the house that the best course of action would be to refer the matter to a parliamentary committee prior to second reading. This did not have the effect of killing the bill, for the very good reason it was a controversial matter upon which many persons in this country wanted to make representations. It was decided to refer it to a committee prior to second reading so that the government would not feel that any substantial changes in that particular legislation would involve any backing down or

votes of non-confidence. I am sorry this course was not adopted in connection with this legislation, but I assume the government has no intention at this stage of changing its course and referring it to a committee before second reading.
After listening to the debate I also resent the approach of some of the speakers, notably those on the government side, which suggests that any members who object to any phase of the pension plan are trying to deprive the lame, the halt, the blind, the widowed and the orphaned from receiving a decent standard of living. This attempt to label anyone who has any criticism to make, be it constructive or not, as some sort of callous monster of the extreme right, places us in an unfortunate position if we honestly try to put forward our objections.
However, I have a proposal to put forward which I think could have been considered by the hon. lady, though she never asked me for advice and I am not surprised about that. I wish to advance a suggestion merely to show there are other possibilities of accomplishing the same sort of things that are involved in Bill C-136.
It seems to me there are five or six principles that any expansion of social security must meet. These are practical principles, assuming we all agree that Canadians want to retire in dignity and decency. The first of these is that a plan must be readily understandable by those who are to receive benefit from it, by those who are to pay for it, and by all Canadians who at one point or another are going to be called on to vote for the government that brings in this plan. There must be a clear understanding of what they are voting for and against.
The second practical principle of any social security scheme is that it must be the best way not only of meeting existing needs but of filling in gaps in the social security program. I recall at the time of my graduation from the British Columbia school of social work that the guest speaker was the then deputy minister of welfare, Dr. Davidson, and he described Canada's social security system as a Joseph's coat of many colours. He was followed on the podium by Dr. R. E. Davis of the Canadian welfare council, a man involved in the day to day administration of welfare, and he said that rather than a Joseph's coat of many colours it might be likened to a good old Canadian patchwork quilt. I mention this because there are many different ways of looking at this and of meeting all the needs. I suggest the Canada pension plan is only one
Canada Pension Plan
of the possibilities and not necessarily the best.
The third practical principle in welfare administration is that the administrative costs of any program must be kept to an absolute minimum so that the bulk of the funds collected go to the people they are designed to help, and so that they are not collected by the government to maintain a huge army of employees taking in each other's paper work.
The fourth practical principle of a federal program is that it must be the same for all Canadians. It must have complete portability no matter where you go and it must be under the control of the same authority. As a Canadian I am not prepared, having gone to another province, to reapply for benefit and to be placed under the control of the provincial authority, and it does not matter which of the ten provinces is concerned.
As a fifth practical principle it must be able to stand the scrutiny of those of us here and now who want to look at it, and it must stand the test of time.
The sixth practical principle in social security is that whatever scheme is introduced must cause a minimum of disruption in the private and public sectors of the economy. I want to state in a paragraph an alternative that I have in mind.
I believe that we would have accomplished suitable care of the elderly by raising old age security payments to $100 a month immediately, by lowering the eligibility to 65 years immediately, by pegging payments to the cost of living, by keeping it a totally federal program with no possibility of opting out, and by financing it through the required increase in the three taxes that now finance it, sales tax, corporation tax and income tax.
In order to meet the needs of another large group who would not be covered by this scheme-because after all I am only talking about those over age 65-in keeping with the request voiced by one province and which had general support, I would suggest that the federal government convene a meeting to look at the whole area of services to the disabled, the blind, and the mother's allowance programs now in effect through the provincial authorities. It should allow these programs to remain under provincial control, with whatever necessary federal guidance and help that would be required by the provinces.
The advantage of my suggestion is that everyone in Canada can understand what $100 a month is. It would be available to everyone, and when I mention pegging it to the cost of living I suggest that the cost of living for

Canada Pension Plan
1965 be equal to 100 points and, not as presently calculated, to 100 points in 1949. Mr. Speaker, if you follow what I am saying you will see that what I am suggesting is that we guarantee to every old person over 65 years $100 a month in purchasing power, no matter what happens to the cost of living from now on.
If my plan were adopted it would not be necessary to increase old age security immediately prior to an election. Everyone would understand the benefit would be $100 a month and the cheques payable would be pegged to the cost of living as of today, not as of 1949. This would have the advantage of payments beginning on a universal basis at the age which is now generally accepted for compulsory retirement. At present there is a gap. In many instances people are compulsorily laid off at age 65 and cannot acquire old age security until they are 70.
I want to read one subclause from the bill, and by no means is it the most complex.

speechtext:
Clause 22(3), relating to contributions to be made by employers and employees, reads as follows:
Where an employer has been informed in writing on behalf of the minister pursuant to an inquiry, other than an application for determination of a question under section 28, that he is not required to make a deduction from the remuneration of an employee under this act and it is subsequently determined or decided under section 28 or 29 that such a deduction should have been made, except where the employer was so informed on the basis of information furnished by him to the minister that was incorrect in a material particular the employer is not liable for failing to make the deduction or for any amount that should have been deducted before the determination or decision is communicated to him, but is thereupon liable, without interest or penalties under this act, to pay the contribution required to be made by him with respect to the employee from whose remuneration the deduction should have been made, and upon payment by the employer of any amount as or on account of the contribution so required to be made by him the employee shall be deemed to have notified the minister as required by paragraph (b) of subsection (1) of section 14 of the employer's failure to deduct that amount from the remuneration of the employee.
Now what in God's name does that mean? I have taken this clause apart phrase by phrase and it is simply not understandable. I suggest that the first requirement of any adequate security program must be that it

can be understood by those who receive benefits, by those who are to pay for them and by the voters at large.
Now I want to get on to my next point. It is that the administrative costs of any plan should be kept to a minimum. Let us look at the plan before us in terms of what it will cost to administer. What would it cost us to number Canadians and keep track of them throughout their working lives? What would it cost us to transfer files from one area to another as people move from one area to another, or to other countries, to work? What will it cost us to determine whether a man is disabled under the terms of this act? This has proved a major source of difficulty and expense already in connection with the Disabled Persons Act. What about the cost of appeals made before the quasi-judicial bodies which will have to be set up to determine blindness, disability, and so on? What about the procedure involved in transferring from the federal program to the provincial program when a province has decided to opt out? Who will transfer these files? What vast army of bureaucrats will be necessary to carry out this work even assuming its members do not engage in empire building and spend all their time watching each other? What army of officials will be needed in every province of this country to keep track of all these things? Compare this with the program I have put forward under which we need keep track of no Canadian until he reaches the age of 65 and establishes his eligibility.
I have said that a program of social security if it is to be effective must be the same for all Canadians. At this point only a single province has decided that it will not implement this plan but that it will implement its own. As a Canadian prepared to pay federal taxes and prepared to be a Canadian, I object to having to place myself or my parents or my children in the future under the control of the provincial authority of any other province of this country. I object to this most strongly when we are using federal funds.
I have said that a social security system must stand scrutiny now and that it must stand the test of time. According to the minister's own paper we do not know what is going to happen in a few years; we cannot carry the projection beyond a few years. By pegging the pension at $100 a month based on the cost of living in 1965 equalling 100, the old people will know what they are going to get. At present many of them think they will be reaping good benefits if this measure

goes through, although in fact if in 1967 the cost of living goes up by 1 per cent a person now in receipt of old age security benefit will end up in receipt of the grand total of 72 cents a month added to his existing pension, enough to handle the correspondence between himself and the local office of the Canada pension plan to find out why he is not getting more.
I have also said that a good social security system must cause the least possible disruption to the private sectors of the economy. Under my plan everyone reaching the age of 65 would be entitled to $100 from the state, and no more. Those who are able to look after themselves and who are fortunate enough to be able to arrange for their own insurance would have that in addition. There would be no need to disrupt a single existing pension plan. The pension or benefit from state sources would amount to $100 and I do not think the state has a responsibility to guarantee any person more than $100 from public funds. Under the proposed Canada pension plan no one knows for certain what the future will bring. We have been given brave assurances by the minister that somehow or other, through some strange Liberal magic, integration of the Canada pension plan with private plans will occur.
I have tried in the brief 15 minutes I have taken to outline one possible alternative to the Canada pension plan, one which would not require a pound and a half of printing to describe it, one which would be understood by every Canadian. It would be understood by every Canadian voter when the time comes to have another go at the polls. This is important because there will be no element of fooling; the people would know. I put forward this suggestion not because I expect the government to accept it but merely because I want to point out as a person trained in the field of welfare and as one with a good deal of experience in administering provincial plans that there are other ways of achieving the benefits which the minister and all of us in this house wish to achieve for Canadians. It is regrettable that the government should refuse to allow this to go before a committee before second reading, where this kind of thing could have been studied and documented. I repeat my request now. If the minister would agree to it, it would at least establish that at least the government is not afraid of taking this particular 125-clause bill to a committee-is not afraid to let it stand the test of close scrutiny.

This is a completely new role of government, certainly in North America.

Whether the public can wisely turn over its life savings to the investment wisdom and political pressures of an elected government is a question which should have the deepest and most thoughtful appraisal-but this is not the time.

Let's raise a storm. Let's make it a good one-the strongest most lightning-packed, angry wind that has blown around parliament hill for a long, long time. It could sober this country as it sorely needs.

Which, of course, is and has been for a long time rather typical of the attitude taken in Canada by Liberal governments. Their general attitude seems to me: Well now, we must be very careful not to do anything to rock the boat. I think the Liberals must have a congenital weakness which makes them liable to seasickness; they are always so afraid of rocking the boat.
I thought the Minister of Finance gave us this afternoon a perfect example of just how touchy he is as far as the dangers of rocking boats are concerned. I suppose I could suggest that there are such things as seasickness pills; and if the Minister of National Health and Welfare could provide as part of the health services for the country some seasickness pills for the members of the government and the members of her own party who are so afraid of rocking boats perhaps she might be able to bring forward a better and more adequate proposal than she has put forward in this bill.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that those who are so concerned or inclined to be concerned about group security plans provided under the aegis of public authority are really people who refuse to recognize or to realize just how radically the structure of our society has changed and how, as one of the consequences of that change, the older generation have tended to be pushed into a sort of side line position in our economy.

I think that the fact of this change was perhaps illustrated by some of the considerations we had in mind when we recently dealt with the redistribution bill. During the discussion it became quite clear, as it has through many other avenues of knowledge, that the structure and economic status of Canadian society has radically changed because of the movement from rural areas into urban areas, and the question of adequate security for old age is part and parcel of that development.
In a simple rural society largely established on an agricultural base the question of security for the aged tended to take care of itself as a result of the rather simple and basic fact that by and large the ownership of the means of production rested in the hands of the older people. In other words, father owned the farm and, while the sons might work it, as long as father was alive he had a proper right, title and interest in the products of the farm. On the other hand, let me take an example that pertains to the area of the country from which I come with regard to the society in which we live today. In the society of today the father no longer owns the pulp mill or the paper mill, and once his active working years are over he has no automatic right, title or interest in the continued production of that pulp or paper mill or in any of the other complex industrial institutions which operate in our society today and which represent our main economic base.
I think it is out of that change in the structure of our society that the need for public pension plans arises which will ensure that the older generation will continue to enjoy some of the fruits of current production. In my view it is in that context that this kind of plan has to be assessed, and it is in the context of the productivity of the industrial machine that the adequacies or inadequacies of proposed levels of pension plans must be considered.
There has been a good deal of talk recently about priorities. Some of it has arisen out of the fairly recent statement by the premier of the province of Manitoba on this subject. A recent newsletter of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce quotes from the statement of Premier Duff Roblin and then proceeds to make certain assertions which they suggest arise out of the premier's statement. They completely overlook the fact that the premier's statement dealt with the matter of a co-operative effort on the part of the provincial and federal governments to assess their sources of revenue and to work out

some co-ordinated plan for the manner in which expenditures are to be made. The chamber of commerce goes far beyond the context of Premier Roblin's remarks. In their newsletter they say:
The newly elected board of directors of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce urges federal and provincial governments to co-operate in establishing priorities in respect to government expenditures.
They go on to say:
It is clear that the tasks which the nation undertakes in the fields of education, old age security, health and other programs affecting the public sector of the economy must be considered and dealt with on a priority basis.
I do not claim to be an economist, Mr. Speaker, but I have enough knowledge of the proper use of economic terms to realize that this statement emanating from the board of directors of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce is utter and complete nonsense. They talk about programs affecting the public sector of the economy as if the public sector of the economy comprised such things as education, health and old age security. To me this is a complete misuse of that term, because as far as I am concerned the public sector of the economy refers to such activities as public enterprises, publicly owned railways or the Polymer Corporation or Air Canada, which are part of the economic life of Canada. To suggest that matters such as education, old age security and health are matters of concern only to the public sector of the economy does not make economic sense to me.
In my view nothing is more important to the private sector of the economy than that we have educated and healthy citizens. In my view nothing is more important to the private sector of the economy than that all Canadian citizens have the kind of incomes which will enable them to purchase the products that our industrial economy is capable of producing.
I have referred to this statement in order to suggest that we in parliament as well as people throughout the country are in danger of putting such questions as old age security, education and health services and the matter of whether or not we can afford them in a completely false perspective. So many people tend to look upon these things as something to be put to one side as luxuries. To me this is a completely false assessment of priorities. The only sound basis of assessing these things is within the total public and private sectors of our
Canada Pension Plan
economy and their potential productive capacity.
Viewed in those terms, Mr. Speaker, and thinking of a proper sense of priorities as to the things which are really necessary I would say, as I said earlier, that it would not be too much so far as the field of old age security is concerned if we were to put together the proposal advanced by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) and the proposal which the hon. member for Northwest Territories made in reference to the increase in old age security. I would suggest that is the least we can do that would be adequate.
I attempted to point this up in a question I addressed to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) when he concluded his remarks last night. I asked him if he would indicate to the house the position of people who are now of retirement age or who will be at the time the proposed pension plan comes into effect. To me this is something that should not go unnoted in the house, because what it means is that we are taking steps now to ensure that some of us who are of age now to benefit from the plan when we reach retirement age will receive the proposed pension. But apparently the government is content to let those who are now of retirement age fall by the wayside, to simply let them go on living in many cases on the verge of want and starvation.
The Indian society of an earlier day on the west coast of Canada at least had a simple and effective means of dealing with the problem of old age. When the people in some of these societies got to the point where they were no longer productive and could not fend for themselves, they had the very happy custom of taking them down to the rocks at the seashore at low tide. They simply left them there until the tide came in to the top of the beach. So far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, this is what we are doing under this plan as it stands. We are simply saying to the people who are now at retirement age, so far as this parliament is concerned we are quite prepared to leave you on the beach at low tide and let you be submerged. If I have one basic criticism of the proposal of the government, it is this niggardliness. I do not believe the Canadian people really want parliament to be this niggardly with these people who are being completely left out except for this very minor modification of old age security being tied to the cost of living.

Canada Pension Plan
I suggest that this nation, on any proper assessment of its economic capacity, on any proper assessment of priorities, should say that it is prepared, as part of this plan, to close that gap either by increasing the present old age pension to an adequate level or by the abbreviation of this transitional period in the Canada pension plan. Through this parliament the people of Canada should pick up the tab for the people now of retirement age or the people now on retirement. So far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, this is the only valid, fundamental criticism of the proposal that we have before us. Certainly I hope that before this plan becomes law or even before the bill passes second reading, we will have an indication that there will be general support in this house for something being done about this aspect of the proposal.

I want to reply to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), Mr. Speaker. He said we were afraid to say where we stand on this pension. I will say that I am for the bill, all the members on this side are for the bill and I believe the same is true of members on the other side of the house.

Mr. Speaker, I would like first of all to commend the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) and the government for their persistency in preparing this bill.
We have heard several hon. members mention that the government presented two, three or four versions of this bill. I wish to commend the government for this attitude which illustrates its broadmindedness.
Had the federal government not taken this action in 1963, there would be no pension plan covering all Canadians, and there would not be any either in the province of Quebec for several years.
It may be said that the federal government had to back-track and to compromise with the government of the province of Quebec but what counts, in the final analysis, is that with this piece of legislation we have reached our goal: a comprehensive pension plan will be established across Canada, from Vancouver to St. John, Newfoundland, a plan which will follow every worker in Canada whenever he transfers to another province to earn his living.
This excellent piece of legislation is vitally important to the mobility of the Canadian labour force because we have often seen people residing, for instance, in eastern

Quebec, go and work for a few months or a few years in New Brunswick; we have often seen people in western Quebec finding employment in northeastern Ontario.
So, this plan which was worked out in cooperation with the provinces, gives Canada a very important security measure and I think this is an important date in the history of social security in this country.
In the last 12 years, we had not had many new measures in the field of social security. In 1952, a general old age pension plan for Canada was inaugurated but between 1952 and 1964, except for the hospital insurance plan, Canada did not do much with regard to social security.
Today, with this pension plan which covers all Canadians, I think that we are taking a great step forward.
It was not an easy task to prepare and draft that bill on account of the many constitutional objections it gave rise to. But because the governments carried out coolheaded discussions a solution was found. Section 94A of the constitution, following the 1951 amendment, allowed the federal government to legislate with regard to pensions. However, that gave prior rights to the provinces if they decided to take the initiative in that field.
When the present government announced its intention to establish a national pension plan, the province of Quebec said that it intended to set up its own plan and, in conformity with the rights it has under the constitution, it evidently was entitled to do so.
In my opinion, from a confrontation of the Quebec and federal plans there resulted appreciable benefits for both. This confrontation greatly improved the federal as well as the provincial plan.
I am not mentioning the pension plan put forward by the province of Ontario, because it was a security plan for insurance companies rather than for workers.

I did not suggest that the pension plan now before us would replace anything. This is a new measure which will be additional to old age security.
As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, the confrontation of those two plans resulted in the improvement of both, the federal one and the provincial one.
Among the social security improvements to be found in the federal plan, there is a capitalization which will be most useful to the federal government as well as to those provinces wishing to use the amounts made available to them for investment purposes, as mentioned in the bill, especially with regard to the investment programs of each of the provinces.
The second improvement brought to the federal plan since its first draft is that it is now compulsory for everybody. All citizens have been put on an equal footing. In my view, it is very important to compel every one to take part in this pension plan, because if they had been free to do so, some individuals would not have taken advantage of this pension plan, and upon reaching the pensionable age, they would have been second class citizens deprived of the protection which every citizen must receive in a relatively modern society.
Another advantage which was brought about by the confrontation of both plans was the extension of this plan to invalids, widows, orphans and also the granting of death benefits. In my opinion, the fact that both plans were compared at a certain time allowed the central government to obtain authorization from the provincial governments to amend the constitution so that the benefits of this pension plan could be extended to those persons who, during their working life, for instance, may become destitute because they were not included in this pension plan.
Then, thanks to this pension plan, these people will receive benefits, even when a member of the family leaves them for a better world.
This is very important for the security of our fellow citizens in general. In my opinion, this improvement was essential. And even if
Canada Pension Plan
this were the only result of the confrontation of the two plans, this event was worth while.
As far as improvements to the Quebec plan are concerned, I could mention the following: first of all, a reduced rate of contribution from 4 per cent in the original Quebec plan to 3.6 per cent.
Another improvement is the reduction of the number of years prior to the date of coming into force of the plan. Under Quebec's original scheme, the act would not have applied to citizens for 20 years. Because it was possible to combine both schemes, the citizens of my province will benefit from that great social security legislation ten years hence. That is a tremendous improvement.
Another advantage I mentioned earlier is the portability of the pension, which means that throughout the country the worker is sure that wherever he goes his pension will go with him. In my opinion, the Quebec worker would not have enjoyed that advantage under his own plan if there had not been an agreement with the federal government. That additional improvement must be greatly appreciated in the province of Quebec.
Both plans also contain a very important principle I want to point out.
This is the first piece of social security legislation which recognizes the very important principle that benefits will increase when the cost of living increases. I think that is a new principle which is being accepted and that in the future it should gain a wider acceptance than in the past because we notice, unfortunately, that social security legislation enacted several years ago has not taken into account the rise in the cost of living, which has considerably reduced its usefulness.
In closing, I think that the federal pension plan now under consideration holds many advantages for the citizens. I am happy to see the bill referred to a committee at this stage so that all its provisions may be studied.
For instance, some complain because the contributions will have to be paid on incomes ranging from $600 to $5,000. It would perhaps be advisable to examine more closely the possibility of increasing it up to $7,000 or $8,000 in order perhaps to reduce the minimum rate, because some labourers who have very low earnings will find it too difficult to contribute to a certain part of the social security provided in the pension plan.
It is true that the minister has amended the plan two or three times and I again

Canada Pension Plan
congratulate her. It is an excellent thing to reach an agreement after some negotiations and nobody must be blamed for reaching a compromise; indeed it has often been said that an arrangement is concluded by two intelligent persons.
We should not withdraw into rigid positions. I want to compliment both governments that looked calmly into the situation and found through constructive negotiations a common ground for the utmost benefit of all Canadian citizens. This constitutional crisis has been settled to the advantage of all Canadians.
Quebec needed funds for its economic development and it got them. The Ottawa government wanted a comprehensive pension plan for all Canadians and we have it. May this example be followed in the future. We should not be ashamed to make a compromise like this one, because we will have in the near future, included in our pension plan, an eminently social measure that the people of my province as well as those from all Canada must welcome wholeheartedly.
