Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few remarks on Bill No. C-136. This bill will put Canadians at the mercy of a government or an institution. It will put them in a strait-jacket and encroach upon their freedom as individuals, either directly or indirectly.
Man, by his very nature, was created free to organize his life according to his aspirations provided they do not harm society. But now the state wants to force Canadian citizens to set aside part of their production and amass something from which they will benefit 52 years hence, that is the period which will elapse between 18 and 70 years of age. And this law is compulsory, if you please, as if it were feared that the earth would quit producing and bearing fruit.
Through this plan, money will pile up, but what exactly will it be used for? Will it not be, for that matter, money which has been taken forcibly? Canadians will be bled white economically, the very minimum requirements for a decent living will be taken away from them, to be used to improve their standard of living 50 years from now.
Mr. Speaker, when I see how little attention the government ministers pay to what we say, I often feel like taking a drastic decision: that of never opening my mouth again in parliament and taking every other available means to fulfil my duties as a member of parliament, as a representative of the

Canadian people and as the member for my district.
However, Mr. Speaker, if hon. members on the treasury benches have ears, but do not hear, and eyes, but fail to see the people's plight, I should, nevertheless, try and raise my voice to a still louder pitch to throw more light upon the matter whenever I get an opportunity.
As far as this Bill No. C-136 is concerned, Mr. Speaker, this considerable effort made by the government further to mislead a suffering and disheartened people, I shall rise once again in the desert of this House of Commons, and this Canadian parliament, which I had thought were more favourably disposed towards the Canadian people.
This famous Canada pension plan bill, in spite of its bombastic title, offers the Canadian people but another opportunity to see their daily bread curtailed, rationed, dried out and shrunk to a mere abstraction, a mere memory or hope; a war-time memory when money was plentiful while blood was flowing in remote parts. Five years of war brought prosperity to the Canadian people and healed the scars of that decade of depression between 1930 and 1940; but, from 1945 to 1965, after 20 years of peace, our whole hard working, peaceful and generous people have gone back to the days of depression, unemployment and destitution.
And to answer the peaceful demands of the people, all the government has to offer is Bill No. C-136. That is all our wise economists, accountants, scientists, experts, engineers and administrators have managed to offer us, the representatives of the people. And you would like us to express satisfaction at such a hazy, cumbersome and devious project as this Canadian pension plan. You are surprised that we do not think of congratulating you for that ridiculous discovery.
Fortunately, ridicule does not kill.
So you do not understand yet that the people no longer want compulsory savings deducted from their salary cheque which is already too small and inadequate for the daily needs of the dedicated worker and his family.
You have not understood as yet that our very presence in this house, we members of the Social Credit, members of the splinter parties, is a popular challenge to your bad political administration; it is a refusal to cooperate in your system which protects the wealth and capital of large institutions and lets a whole people starve or die of misery and poverty while producing plenty? Will such

conditions go on forever? Have not the people reached as yet the end of their hardship and misery? They will have to accept one more deduction from their daily earnings, so that the governments may pile up billions of dollars from the pittance of the people who lack the necessities of life.
What else can we do? Have we not tried everything to open your eyes? Have we not offered various plans which could at least get your attention and your appreciation? But no, our only appreciation is your mockery, when it is not your contempt. Never mind. We are forging ahead just the same. A day will come, which is not far, I hope, when common sense and the natural intelligence of the people will upset once and for all not only the whole system of those bad pieces of legislation intended to pile up capital to the detriment of the human being, but also those schemes, those hindrances which further reduce the freedom of individuals, and especially of the Canadian citizens.
Just imagine a young man 18 years old, earning his first dollars and going into the world full of hopes, not yet entitled to vote, who sees that a deduction is made from his small salary so that he may get a pension when he reaches 70 years of age. Fifty two years later. Old age is not his main worry. He is forced to make a sacrifice today in order to reap crumbs at the end of his career when he reaches 70.
I suppose that your pension plan, as it stands and as it will be applied, will raise further the cost of production and reduce the purchasing power of the people.
What was already wrong is now still worse. Consumers' revenues will decrease and the cost of production will increase all for the purpose of increasing government capital when the government has the power to create capital through the Bank of Canada.
But no, the government prefers to further reduce the purchasing power of the Canadian people. It is more in line with the absurdity of our present system. This absurdity must always be preserved since it is serving the purpose of a few.
Out of an annual production of $46 billion, we allow a few Canadians to pile up profits and capital amounting to $14 billion after paying taxes and making a good living, but we do not want the small earner to enjoy even the bare necessities of life. It would be too dangerous if the people had security. This surplus must be taken away from them even before they have a chance to look at it. It is taken from them even 20220-645
Canada Pension Plan
before they cash their pay cheques. They are being deprived of it without ascertaining whether or not they need it for their own children, to buy them shoes. But that does not enter into the picture at all. We must at all costs increase the capital of our poor governments who entrust others with the power to create money, capital, under any possible debt forms.
Imagine, besides, that this Canadian pension plan, which deprives the poor in Canada of their daily bread, will serve to increase the pension of the wealthy, who have already all the necessary reserves to ensure their old age. It is not without any reason that we find in the gospel: "Who hath not from him shall be taken and whosoever hath to him shall be given."
The writers of those days already saw what was going to happen in Canada in 1964 at the federal government level under the leadership of Christian ministers, defenders of the faith in Christ.
Now, imagine, Mr. Speaker, that in this Canada pension plan no thought is even given to all our Canadian citizens. Our citizens will not all be entered on this pension list. A great number of them will still lack the essentials of life and will not benefit from this pension plan. What will you do then with those citizens who have none the less to defend themselves against the mishaps of destiny, this famous bill of rights guaranteeing to each individual in Canada his right to life, freedom, security of the person? Go and see, I invent nothing. Look up the Canadian Bill of Rights, which was passed unanimously by the 265 members, without any exception, of the parliament of Canada, where it is declared that each citizen is entitled to life, to the necessities of life, but where care is taken not to say that each citizen is entitled to the amount of money necessary to his life, his freedom, his subsistence.
And yet, what can we do without money? Would the ministers themselves have been able to get elected without the fabulous sums that elections cost? Where does this money come from? But to secure a strict minimum for Canadian citizens, it is impossible to guarantee each Canadian citizen the minimum amount required.
If we have the right to live, if the pension payable under the Canada pension plan is a strict minimum, even inadequate for a decent living, why are we required to pay more money for what is already a recognized right in our legislation? Why make anyone pay for

Canada Pension Plan
something which is already recognized as a right of each individual in Canada?
Is a dog obliged to pay to have the right to live?
Mr. Speaker, only man, that proud and superior animal, is subjected to that vile and degrading slavery. Only man, among all God's creatures, is obliged at 18 to start saving for the time when he is 70, if he lives that long. Only man is thus obliged to provide against God's kindness.
That is to explain, Mr. Speaker, why science is only the third of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit or the Holy Ghost, as you wish. It is just as good if not better than party spirit.
God's wisdom, or God in His wisdom, has given the earth the power to produce all that is required for the nourishment of all its inhabitants, yearly and for every year.
Our monetary, economic and political systems should abide by this will of God that is so well expressed in nature. I was going to say in the Bible, but nature is, still more than the Bible, the word of God. Nature is rather the act of God, than the word.
When in your Canada pension plan you are asking, you are requiring an 18 year old boy, who is not yet entitled to vote to start paying taxes out of a meagre salary, so as to save money in order to get the benefit of it in 52 years, when he is 70 years old perhaps, if he is still living at that time, in the year 2016, you are guilty of a sacrilege, a sacrilege against God, against his Bible, against his gospel, against your oath of allegiance.
When a young man has not enough money to live decently at the present time, to marry, to carry on his studies, if he so wishes, you force him to put aside certain sums which will serve to pile up billions of dollars- according to the Minister of National Health and Welfare $8 billion will be accumulated in ten years-I submit that this is disgraceful. In fact, I believe that as Canadians, as representatives of the people, if we cannot find a more logical formula which would be more acceptable to the people, it would be preferable for us to resign and go back home, because not one of us deserves to represent the people.
Those were the remarks I wanted to make, Mr. Speaker.

This is exactly what happens under the Canada pension plan. People who can serve another ten years of pensionable employment from the date the plan comes into

Canada Pension Plan
operation will be able to get full benefits when they retire, even though the benefits they are to receive would be far in excess of their contributions. Therefore the Canada pension plan, in the same way as private plans, recognizes the past service of employees, the contribution they have made to their country, and permits them to receive full benefits. This certainly cannot be considered an unfair burden on our younger people who will be contributing to the plan for a long period. After all, they have benefited from the efforts of those who are now reaching retirement age. In any event, it would not be correct to say that the difference between the amounts contributed by those who do receive full benefit at the end of the transition period and the amounts of these pensions would be paid solely by the younger people. This difference would undoubtedly be made up, at least in part, by contributions from employers.
However, the argument has still been made that in creating the Canada pension plan we will be placing future generations in a situation where they have an overly onerous burden placed upon their shoulders, forcing them to pay the costs of the benefits which we may be establishing today. But this plan's approach is basically the same as that of our existing old age security system under which those now working pay for the old age pension of those who are retired; and the same can be said to apply with respect to our other existing social welfare benefits- that those not getting them help pay for those who are, to the benefit of the entire population. If the contributions of those who come after will pay for the pensions of those already retired, they in turn will be in the same situation.
The minister in her speech on second reading pointed out the unlikelihood of an increase in contribution rates for a generation; but if after 20 years some increase does become necessary surely it will be no different from increasing taxes, as we have done from time to time, to bring about needed increases in existing old age security pensions. I am sure that, as is the case today, members of future generations will be more concerned with the percentage of their income which they pay to the plan and the benefits they receive from it than the possibility that they are also helping to pay for benefits for others.
This Canada pension plan finally before us has also been subject to criticism because it provides for the building up of a sizeable fund in its initial stages which will be

available to the provinces in proportion to the contributions from them. It seems curious to me that some of this criticism has appeared to come from some of the very same people who criticized the complete pay as you go basis of the first version of this plan on the ground that it was not actuarially sound. While in this house we cannot attribute motives to speakers within its walls I do not suppose that there is anything to prevent us from doing so with regard to those who criticize in this way legislation of this type. In any event, there has been a lot of discussion lately about priorities of government expenditure, what should come first, whether it should be pensions or education or medical care. But this question cannot be answered by fixing on only one of these needs to the complete exception of all the others. The sick, the aged, the young are all part of our society, as they always will be. None of them can be ignored completely while another group is being looked after.
Therefore, the priorities can only be priorities of emphasis and of degree. You cannot decide that for the next ten years, for example, you will spend money only on schools and nothing on pensions. Some way must be found to meet these needs to one extent or another. The building up of a fund from the contributions made during the initial years of the Canada pension plan provides a way, at least a partial way, of dealing with this question of priorities for the next several decades, of harmonizing seemingly conflicting needs of different segments of our population, all of which have a right to be taken care of to some degree at the same time.
I wonder if I might call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

There has been a tremendous demand for schools arising out of our rapidly expanding population and its need to adapt to changing technology. This same population has created a similar demand for hospital facilities and these are considered amongst the most pressing needs for social capital. However these fields fall under the responsibility of the provinces and are likely to do so certainly for the immediate future. To meet these demands for social capital today the provinces must have the necessary finances. The Canada pension plan provides a way for them to

obtain these finances and at the same time enables Canadians to begin providing for themselves a reasonable, basic standard of income for their retirement years.
Some concern has been expressed over the implication of making available these sizeable investment funds to governments, and at having them left in the hands of politicians. While I am not suggesting that all politicians are above reproach, at the same time I cannot accept the argument that all elected representatives in Canada today, aided by their civil service advisers, are generally speaking any less responsible or sound in their judgments than business executives, among whom have been found some who have made decisions which led not only to loss of money on the part of their firms but to actual bankruptcy.

maintopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR EQUALIZATION OF WELFARE PAYMENTS
INDIAN AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR EQUALIZATION OF WELFARE PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I asked the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration if he would allay the fears of many native Indian people across the country by announcing the government's policy with respect to the amounts of welfare benefit payments to these people in order that the Indian people of Canada will not be enticed into the field of provincial jurisdiction by higher welfare payments when they may not want to participate in the provincial plan.
On November 2, the minister answered a number of questions posed by myself and other members of the house about the procedure to be followed after the dominion-provincial conference on Indian affairs was held. The minister stated, as reported on page 9652 of Hansard:


Firstly, in every province of Canada, there shall be held a conference to which all Indians will be invited so they can express their wishes and their suggestions on the very principle of extending provincial services to the Indians in every province.
The first thing these native people would like to know, Mr. Speaker, is who is going to arrange for this conference? How are the native people going to get there? Who is going to pay the costs of the conference, the costs of transportation and the like, of the native people to attend this particular conference? They would like to know that. However, that is incidental to the main point.
I continue to quote from the minister's statement:
After this consultation and provided the Indians agree that such provincial services would be desirable, there shall be a second method consultation; the bands will be consulted. Every band in Canada or in every province will be consulted-
Then he went on to say that every band in Canada or in every province would be consulted, that is the councils of those bands would be consulted, in order to ascertain if they wished to take advantage of a program to be established in a province, and every band which did not wish to take advantage of provincial services would be free to reject such services. Under those circumstances, the federal services would remain in force.
We do know that there are native Indian people in different parts of Canada who strenuously object to having jurisdiction over their affairs dealt with in any way by provincial governments. There are Indian people in other parts of Canada who believe it would be desirable to have jurisdiction over their affairs dealt with in the same way as everybody else, and that there be equality of application of the law. This situation is likely to develop. A native Indian or a group of native Indians may not want, for the sake of argument, to have jurisdiction over welfare services dealt with by the provincial government. It may well be that the provincial government is paying welfare payments greatly in excess of the niggardly amounts paid by the Indian affairs branch. What they would like to know is if the government will declare that welfare payments payable to native Indian people will be on a par with those made by the various provinces so that this monetary enticement will not be held out to them by the provinces in order to entice the Indian people to come under provincial jurisdiction. This is a serious matter.
Recently, for instance, in British Columbia one of the Indian superintendents, speaking

at a conference of the Nishga tribal council on January 1, said the Indian affairs branch would make welfare payments on the same basis as those payments are made by the provincial authorities. This is a welcome announcement. It should have been made many years ago. We would like to know if this is the policy of the government in all of these provinces. Will they treat the Indian people on a basis of equality in so far as the various services are concerned which might be provided by the provinces, and which they might accept at this conference which is about to be arranged? They want to know where they stand. They do not want to be bought off or have it look as if they are being bought into provincial jurisdiction. If this were to be the case, it would be a most disgraceful state of affairs, to have a province offer money to the native people to get them to come under their jurisdiction and relinquish what they feel in their hearts are their rights under the crown, and under the jurisdiction of the government of Canada.

ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-INQUIRY AS TO ESTABLISHMENT OF APPEAL BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on July 27 I asked the Minister of Justice, who I am disappointed not to see in his seat tonight particularly because of the gravity with which I view the situation, to provide an answer to this question. On that date I suggested that the minister give consideration to setting up an appeal board procedure similar to that which is used in the armed forces court martial appeal board, so that there could be impartial and rapid disposal of charges which have been brought against members of the R.C.M.P. under rules which at best can be described as rather archaic.
The minister said he would consider the matter as one for government policy. I presume the parliamentary secretary will be answering for him tonight and I wish to suggest it is a matter of great urgency, as pointed out by the recent developments in Montreal with respect to two highly placed officers, one the commanding officer of the whole subdivision, who have been dealt with by a trial procedure and convicted.
An appeal was brought before three other officers, as is the procedure under the act. The appeal was dismissed and a recommendation was made by the commissioner of the mounted police, which the minister has not yet dealt with, notwithstanding the fact that it was made shortly before Labour day. For two and a half months these officers and their families have been kept in suspense waiting upon the minister's decision. The minister has to decide, of course, whether or not to recommend to his cabinet colleagues that the recommendation of the commissioner be carried out. I put it to the parliamentary secretary that this procedure is archaic. It is time it was changed. Justice delayed is justice denied and no further delay can be justified in this particular case.
It has not been my intention to jeopardize the individuals concerned or the good reputation which the R.C.M.P. enjoys not only in
10206	HOUSE OF
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion this country but throughout the world. But national press stories, particularly one which appeared on November 13 in the Toronto Star, have now publicized details of the case and it is time the minister or someone in authority spoke up. Any further delay would amount to a complete neglect of the responsibility which the minister has for making a decision. Since the recommendation was made, two and a half months have gone by and the individual officers concerned should not, in my opinion, be held any longer in suspense with regard to the unfortunate developments which have placed them in the position in which they now find themselves and their families. An impartial appeal procedure similar to that available to the armed forces would do away with this kind of injustice.
My purpose in raising this matter on July 17 continues to be my purpose. As matters have developed there appears to be a need for the minister to say something which will restore morale which has deteriorated seriously within the force. I see the parliamentary secretary laughing at that, but I am serious when I say to him that the morale of the force has been jeopardized by this delay. The minister has a responsibility to restore it. It does not take two and a half months for all the surrounding circumstances to be investigated so that the minister can reach a decision. I know I shall probably be told that all the surrounding circumstances are being investigated and that when this investigation has been completed an announcement will be made. But even if only two months had elapsed there would have been ample time for the minister to have acted responsibly.
The delay is having a serious effect also on the confidence placed by the minister in the commissioner of the R.C.M.P. who made the recommendation based on the advice of four senior officers of the force. Either the minister has confidence in the commissioner or he has not. It is time this house and the public knew. It would also be good for the morale of individuals in the force if they, too, knew how the minister stands in this regard.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. S. Macdonald (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-INQUIRY AS TO ESTABLISHMENT OF APPEAL BOARD
speechtext:
It seems to me there are two things to be said with respect to the hon. member's observations tonight. The first is that it is a sad and grave misfortune both for the individuals involved in this particular situation and for the proud service to which they belong that these incidents should have arisen. I know all right thinking people would agree that the fact these circumstances have come to pass should
[Mr. Nielsen.)

not be the basis for any type of unfair yellow journalism or for any type of political exaggeration.
It comes as a surprise to me that the hon. member should have described the rules as archaic and the procedure as being out of date, because he should know that the statute which governs this situation was enacted by parliament in 1959, at a time when the hon. member was a member of this house and a supporter of the government of the day and if, indeed, the rules are as fraught with injustice as he maintains, it is extraordinary he should have sat through that debate so supinely and done nothing to assert what seems to him now to be a basic principle. If this was not evident to the hon. member in 1959 it should certainly have been evident to him and to the government he supported in 1961.
I would refer the house to the case of re Walsh and Jordan, reported in volume 31 Dominion Law Reports, second series, 1962, at page 88, a justice of the Ontario high court held that the Canadian Bill of Rights had no application to the procedure which was involved in that case, which also related to disciplinary action against an officer of the R.C.M.P. It was held that this much-vaunted statute was here again just a dead letter and had no application. If indeed the government which the hon. gentleman supported felt at that time that there was a question of justice involved here, one would have expected they would have taken some action on it. However, I think a further important characteristic here is that you are involved in the cases of two men with, respectively, 34 years and 15 years service in this force. I do not think any member present who stops to reflect on these matters would want any kind of drumhead justice-would want them to lose, for example, the pension rights which they have accrued-without a full consideration of their cases.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-OTTAWA VALLEY-EMERGENCY LEGISLATION RESPECTING DROUGHT CONDITIONS
AGRICULTURE-OTTAWA VALLEY-EMERGENCY LEGISLATION RESPECTING DROUGHT CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I asked a question of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) and, in his absence, the parliamentary secretary with regard to the very serious situation of drought which exists in eastern Ontario generally and in Renfrew county in particular. Yesterday the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) asked a question with regard to a similar situation which apparently exists

in Pontiac, in the province of Quebec. At that time the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve), who replied to the question, felt that some action should be taken in this regard by the province of Quebec.
I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that this matter is of some national moment as well as of great importance to the farmers of Renfrew county, by reason of the statement of the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose (Mr. Smallwood), who indicated that the forcible sale of cattle by farmers of eastern Ontario, and in particular Renfrew county where the drought is most severe, might result in affecting cattle prices across the nation as a whole. I think, therefore, the problem is one which affects not only the particular area of drought, which is largely in Renfrew and Lanark counties, but possibly the national economy in so far as it pertains to the sale and price of cattle across the country. I would point out that I appreciate there is a constitutional difficulty in these matters; that unfortunately national legislation pertaining to crises in various provinces where, through no fault of their own the farmers of this country are very hard hit by drought or other disasters of this nature which stem from an act of God, is possibly lacking in this parliament by reason of the fact that to date no national policy has been evolved with the co-operation of the provinces.
However, Mr. Speaker, I do submit that in a situation such as this, which affects not only the economic well-being of these farmers but even involves the possibility of the wells being dry and the water tables being extremely low, and which might affect the question of health and welfare in these areas, surely when a crisis of this kind occurs some action can be taken under the federal powers to remedy it. This is a very serious situation which exists in the counties of Renfrew and Lanark by reason of the very serious drought existing at the present time and the very bad conditions with regard to the wells and water tables. I would point out that the entire season has been dry to the extent that the hay crop has been short, so that at the present time feed is extremely short. Accordingly these farmers have to sell cattle at below their market value almost on a forced sale basis. Not only will this create very serious economic difficulties for them but it will possibly depress the market generally.
I would also point out the serious emergency situation existing not only with respect to cattle but with regard to the tobacco growers of the area. Theirs is very nearly a 20220-646
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion total loss this year by reason of the drought, and I suggest that some action should be taken by the department not only to remedy the situation regarding the shortage of hay, but to enable these unfortunate tobacco farmers to recover from the blow they have suffered. I may say that tobacco farming in this area is in its infancy. I think it is well known that this area is not a rich economic area. It is an economic area where any industry, such as tobacco farming, which is beginning to show some signs of good prospects, should be encouraged. Total loss in one of the early years could prove fatal to this burgeoning industry.
The Minister of Agriculture has displayed, I think, a dynamism and capacity for action. I think he has come to be known as the farmers' C. D. Howe, and it is to be hoped that in a situation such as this some action will be forthcoming along the lines we have become accustomed to from the dynamic Minister of Agriculture who is in office at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to the hon. member for Renfrew South for bringing this important matter to the attention of all hon. members. I wish to offer him my congratulations for his very deep concern for the farmers of his constituency. This provides me with an opportunity to restate the policy of the government and also to relate some first hand experiences which I had with you, Mr. Speaker, in the county of Stormont, where I had the opportunity of viewing some of the serious conditions existing in your county, which I know are typical of the problem areas of eastern Canada.
The policy of the government, as was the policy of previous governments, has been that the federal government should not interfere unless requested to do so by the province concerned. A province would not normally ask for federal assistance unless it felt that any loss occasioned was beyond their financial capacity to absorb. But the federal government has recognized that many of these problem areas do present a serious drain on the finances of the provinces and therefore the government has been only too willing to enter into consultations with the provinces and to reach agreement on a policy whereby federal assistance can be made available, provided the province concerned initiates the request. The policy is simply that the federal government and the province concerned

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion would enter into an agreement whereby they would pay collectively 75 per cent of the cost of transportation of fodder into these areas up to a maximum of $10 per ton. In addition, the federal government would assist the provinces in paying the transportation of livestock back to the market. This, of course, clearly places a responsibility for initiating any measure of assistance in drought stricken areas on the province.
I think there is also one other responsibility here and I make this statement entirely on my own.
